en: The Sūtra on Birth, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
1. The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Nala. The First [Sūtra].
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a son of noble family who abandoned his home, renounced his wife and children, and left behind all his kinsmen to become a śramaṇa.
His wife was exceptionally beautiful; seeing her husband leave home to become a śramaṇa, she then remarried.
Upon hearing this, the son of good family immediately conceived this thought:
"When I was enjoying myself with my wife, we engaged in the rituals of husband and wife, laughing and playing with heedless abandon.
His mind constantly dwelt upon this, not for even a moment; he thought of his wife before him—her facial features, her physical form, and her manner of sitting, rising, and moving.
Filled with grief, anxiety, and distress, he no longer took pleasure in the pure cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya) and returned to his home.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they went to inform the Buddha.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately sent someone to summon the bhikṣu to come.
They immediately accepted the instruction.
When the bhikṣus arrived, they all paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew to sit on one side.
The Buddha then, for the sake of the bhikṣus, eliminated thoughts of sensual desire and removed the loss caused by delusion and craving, and preached to them as follows:
“The defilements of worldly toil bring little joy but much sorrow; they mostly lead to ruin and seldom to success, and there is no limit to them.
Only the Buddha and his disciples who possess clear wisdom can discern them as such.”
"The offenses born of sensual desire are beyond measure; transcend physical lust, bring rest to all conceptualizations, and dwell in seclusion to discourse upon the Truth.
At that time, the son of noble family immediately realized and verified the Dharma of the Worthy and Holy Ones.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having attained what they had never experienced before, deliberated among themselves, saying: "Let us observe this.

Thereupon, these sons of noble family have abandoned their homes—which are like prisons—along with their heavy shackles and fetters; yet they still harbor thoughts of their wives and children, binding themselves by their own accord and taking no pleasure in the holy life (brahmacarya).
At that time, the World-Honored One revealed the phrases of the Tathāgata:
"The phrases of universal wisdom; the phrases of those with vision; the transformation of persons into worthies and sages.
Then the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"We observe this son of good family who, having renounced his home and become a śramaṇa out of faith, still dwells upon the appearance, movements, and domestic affairs of his wife and children."
The World-Honored One spoke for him, saying:

"The blemish of craving and desire, the virtue of the Dharma and Vinaya, the hardship of birth and death, and the peace of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); [he taught this] so that he might attain the realization of the Sage and reach the realm of non-attachment."
"If it were not for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who else could do such a thing?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This bhikṣu was not only in this present life one whose mind constantly dwells on desire, who is deluded by sensual passion and unable to exercise self-restraint; his will has been bound to desire since time immemorial, and none but the Buddha could transform him, removing his delusions and attachments to love and lust."
In the distant past, long ago, there was a king named Fangji (Square Footprint).

His palace ladies and court maids were beyond counting; they were of upright countenance and peerless beauty. They would quarrel with one another—some with wanton women, abandoning compassion; some with maidservants, or with young boys—and thus they fought and disputed, refusing to live in harmony. Having thus engaged in their quarrels, they would immediately depart from the palace.
When the King first heard of this, he was filled with resentment.
His ministers and officials sought out the palace women, who did not know where he had gone;

they were sorrowful and unhappy, weeping in grief as they remembered the women, their playful laughter and amusements, the duties of husband and wife when they were together, and the various musical performances and the manner of his movements, sitting, and rising—all these thoughts only increased their distress, and they could not console themselves.

At that time, there was a seer who possessed the five supernormal powers, traveling through the air by means of his spiritual feet; his majestic power was boundless, and his name was Nala (in the Jin language, "Without Pleasure").
Seeing King Fangji (Dīpaṃkara) deluded by lustful desire and unable to liberate himself, he gave rise to compassion and wished to eliminate the affliction of that desire.
Flying through the air, he manifested his supernormal powers and suddenly descended, standing upon the king’s palace.
At that time, the king saw him immediately and rose to meet him; he offered him his own couch, and the visitor sat down.
He asked the king:
"Great King, for what reason do you set your heart on sensual desires, laboring with many anxious thoughts and dwelling on the passions of form and color, unable to admonish yourself?"
I bow my head and truly say:

"The ladies of the palace have been contending with one another over their ranks of honor and precedence; unable to reach an accord, they have each fled in different directions. For this reason, I am filled with grief and cannot find relief."
Thereupon the seer explained for him:

"The difficulty of sensual desire and the virtue of renouncing desire: worldly people seek after desires without ever knowing contentment; even if a single person were to obtain all desires, they would still have neither satiety nor fulfillment."
He spoke in verse:
"All the desires of the world—no single person is ever satiated with them.
Since they all bring harm, why do you destroy yourself?"
All the various streams of the world flow entirely toward the ocean, yet it does not consider itself satisfied; so too is that which is loved never satiated.
Even if one were to become a Brahmā, attaining a noble and majestic status difficult to reach—
Desiring to surpass even that, one never feels weary or satisfied.
Even if one were to burn all the trees, grasses, and leaves of Jambudvīpa, one would not be satiated; such is the lack of satiety in desire.
Suppose there were eight types of men, handsome and with beautiful countenances,
all endowed with desire, powerful, and upright. Even if one were to speak words that increase their malice and disparage desire in these men, [it would not cause them to waver].
One does not regard what is light as light, nor does one find weariness in what has not yet become wearying.
Great King, you should know this: if one indulges in the affairs of sensual desire, craving increases all the more, just like drinking salt water.
"At that time, the seer preached for King Dīrghāyus,
reciting verses on the hardships of life to bring about the king's understanding and liberation of mind.
Thus, the seer converted King Dīrghāyus through these teachings of the Dharma.

At that time, the king immediately attained liberation; having no further longing or delight for worldly things, he left the household life to practice the Way. He cultivated the four Brahma-vihāras, severed all craving and desire, and perfected all noble practices.
When his life came to an end, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who the King Dīpaṃkara was at that time, it was this very bhikṣu here; as for the seer Nārada, he was myself."
"At that time we encountered one another, and now we have met again.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was no one who did not rejoice.
2. *The Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Who Begs for Alms* Spoken by the Buddha, Second. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
There was a certain bhikṣu who, while wandering for alms, proceeded in regular succession from house to house until he entered the home of a lecherous woman.

At that time, seeing the bhikṣu enter her house, the courtesan was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; she immediately rose from her seat, went forth to meet him, prostrated at his feet, and invited him to enter and take a seat.
He asked again:
"Bhikṣu! From where have you come?"
The bhikṣu replied, "I am my master’s attendant for alms; therefore, I have come to beg.
At that moment, the woman prepared various kinds of delicacies and savory dishes, filled his bowl to the brim, and presented it to him.
The bhikṣu accepted it and withdrew.
At that time, having obtained such delicious, sweet, and abundant food, his heart was filled with joy beyond measure; he went repeatedly to the house of the courtesan.
At that time, the woman thought to herself,
"In my estimation, this bhikṣu’s adherence to the Dharma is difficult to equal.
She repeatedly prepared sweet, crisp, and succulent foods and presented them to him.
Coming and going without ceasing, his learning remains unclarified, his tasks remain unaccomplished, and he has not yet subdued his sense faculties.
Upon seeing a licentious woman of exquisite beauty, his lustful mind is stirred and his will becomes intent on dissipation.

He became attached to a wanton woman; with words of softness and affection issuing from his mouth and a heart full of intimacy, he conversed with her and frequented her household daily without ceasing.
When a *piṇḍapātika* bhikṣu beholds beautiful forms and hears pleasant sounds, his lustful mind becomes disordered; he is deluded and confused, unable to awaken himself.
Thus the Buddha’s sūtra says:
"When the eyes behold beautiful forms, the lustful mind is stirred."
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"Even when one sees women—those of high status are regarded as mothers;
those of middle status are regarded as elder sisters;"
Those who are young are like sisters, like sons, or like daughters.
One should inwardly contemplate the body, mindful that it is entirely foul and nothing to be desired; outwardly it is like a painted vase, yet its interior is filled with impurities.
"Observe these four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—which are compounded through causes and conditions and are fundamentally non-existent.

At that time, that bhikṣu did not understand the contemplation of emptiness, but viewed them merely as physical forms; his mind was then disturbed by lustful intent, and for the sake of the lustful woman, he spoke this verse:
"The noble lady is young and pure as a child; her countenance is upright, exquisite, and most beautiful.
Beholding each feature of her appearance, there is none like it; my will and aspiration are in perfect accord with hers."
At that time, the wanton woman, seeing that the bhikṣu had spoken thus, thought:

"I originally did not know him to be so cruel, greedy, and lustful; instead, I treated him with a pure mind of upholding the precepts, regarding him as benevolent and virtuous, yet he delights in committing transgressions."
"According to whatever he says, you should respond with refutation.
He then immediately replied with a verse:
"You should bring food and drink, Incense, flowers, and fine garments."
"Only after performing various kinds of offerings shall you accompany the Benevolent One.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu answered the woman in verse, saying:
"I possess no wealth or property; observe my conduct and movements."
"Since you stand by begging, whatever you obtain, let us share it.
Thereupon, the courtesan spoke in verse:
"If your body possesses no wealth or means, why do you set your mind on seeking that which is so difficult to attain?"
"Since you act without shame as you have done, run away quickly and leave my house!
At that time, the bhikṣu was driven out and pursued as far as the gate of Jetavana.
The bhikṣus immediately went to the Buddha and informed the World-Honored One, recounting the matter from beginning to end.
The Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu was formerly a water turtle in a past life, and the courtesan was formerly a monkey; therefore, they are so well-suited to one another."
His aspirations failing to bear fruit, he turns back upon himself in self-deception; not entering the True Teaching, he only increases his afflictions and distress.
Even now it is thus: he set his heart on a courtesan, but when his wishes were not granted and he was met with insult and humiliation, he departed in shame.
The Buddha said:

"In the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a place where turtles dwelt and swam in the waters of a great river. Along the banks of that river, the trees grew lush and thick; within those groves, there was a monkey who lived in one of those trees."
At that time, the turtle emerged from the river water and saw the monkey from afar among the trees; he spoke with him and, gradually moving forward, sought to draw near, coming and going repeatedly.

There will be days when we meet; if we gaze upon one another every day in this manner without ceasing, lustful thoughts will arise, the mind will become deluded, and it will be defiled and turbid, such that one cannot awaken to it oneself.
Then, at that time, he praised him with a verse, saying:
"Your countenance is reddish-yellow and your eyes are blue; you roam among the groves of trees, playing upon the branches.
I now wish to ask about the smoothness of your fur: what do you aspire to, and where do you intend to abide?"
The monkey replied in verse:
"I now fully know the beginning and end of your story; As a prince of the kingdom, you possess great intelligence.
Why do you now question me?"
"Upon hearing these words, I was filled with doubt.
Thereupon, the turtle replied in verse:
"My heart has always held its resolve upon you; My mind harbors love and cherishes constant thought of you."
"For this reason I ask you: by what means may we come together?
The monkey replied in verse, saying:
"Turtle, you should know that I dwell in the trees; I ought not to meet with you."
"If you wish to be with me, We shall dwell among the thickets and provide for one another.
Thereupon the turtle replied in verse:
"What I consume for sustenance is flesh; It is more tender and sweet than fruits and melons."
"You should not greedily seek that which cannot be obtained; I shall instead provide you with many mango fruits.
At that time, the monkey replied in verse:
"If your body were not perched upon the tree, why would you seek from me that which cannot be brought to you?"
"Now, seeing me without shame or remorse, you flee away, unable to bear the sight.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The monkey at that time was this licentious woman; the turtle was the bhikṣu who went for alms."
"At that time, he was negligent and pursued it with longing, yet he did not obtain it as he wished; now it is the same.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there were none who did not rejoice.
3. The Sūtra on the Discourse of Upāli Spoken by the Buddha. Third. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, Upāli the Śākya son sought many followers; without examining the person or scrutinizing their conduct, anyone who wished to leave the household life would have their hair and beard shaved and become a śramaṇa.

When bestowing the precepts of accomplishment, one does not inquire as to their origins or where they come from, the names or lineage of their parents, whether they are good or evil, handsome or ugly, or even whether one knows them or not.
One simply desires to receive the person and, having shaved off their beard and hair, confers the full ordination.
The bhikṣus rebuked him, saying: "You should not do this!
As soon as someone comes along, you immediately ordain them as a śramaṇa, desiring to gather a following while disregarding future calamities."
"You should ask him about his origins and where he has come from; his movements are so composed and deliberate—surely he must have been deceived by someone, for it will be too late for regret.
Yet the bhikṣu Huinán did not accept this advice at all; whenever he saw someone, he would immediately shave off his beard and hair.

At that time, there was a wicked man, the son of a gambler, who heard from afar that the son of the Śākya clan, Vairaṭīputra, possessed countless robes, bowls, and utensils; he sought to gather followers and would accept anyone who came to study under him.
Without inquiring as to their origins or where they had come from, he immediately shaved off their hair and beards.
Their bodies were hungry and cold, and having no means to sustain themselves, they desired to go about deceiving others, their minds already preoccupied with devising schemes.

He went to where Huinàn was, with profound reverence and solemnity, bowing his head in salutation; his deportment and conduct were in accordance with the Dharma, and whether sitting or rising, he was composed and tranquil, without any abruptness or violence.
Vairaṭīputra said to that man:
"The śramaṇa is at peace, free from sorrow and affliction; yet to draw near to sensual desires is not auspicious, for it leads to indolence and a lack of practice."
Those who do not understand are ruined by desire; they habituate themselves to craving and lust, thereby bringing upon themselves the harm of countless afflictions.
Clinging greedily to sensual desires, they are unable to attain liberation.
The man replied, “I am unable to cast off sensual desire and become a śramaṇa.
Upāli asked again:
"My son, for what reason do you not become a śramaṇa?
A śramaṇa gains many benefits; you should humble your mind and go forth as a śramaṇa, and I shall provide all that you require for your practice of virtue."
The man replied, "I accept and obey your command;
having been relieved of all my anxieties and afflictions, if I may find peace and security, I shall become a śramaṇa.
He then shaved off his hair and beard and received the full precepts of ordination.

Although he has become a śramaṇa, he is easy to instruct and guide; therefore, he manifests himself as respectful and compliant without fail, practicing with diligence and never becoming indolent. He is patient and follows the teachings; his character is harmonious, rare to encounter, trustworthy, and reliable.
He did not observe her internal state nor harbor any further doubt; he believed her as if she were one with himself, and entrusted to her all his robes, bowls, and various articles of offering.
Wandering abroad, his mind was at ease.

Without making a display of himself, he gathered up his robes, bowl, and all his requisites for offerings, fled in haste to hide away, and remained alone in one place, eating and drinking together with gamblers.
At that time, Huìnán heard where his new disciple was located and immediately returned in haste. Upon inspecting the room, he saw that many items had been stolen.

He questioned everyone around him extensively: "Where has he gone? He is currently not to be seen. I have only heard reports from afar that this gambler is a fallen, violent man who feigns being a śramaṇa; he wishes to deceive you and steal your property."
The crowd replied, "Your nature is impulsive;

without inquiring into the beginning or the end, you have already shaved off your hair and beard. As for the items you took, they were in a secluded place where gamblers were gathered, and we were eating and drinking together."
"Knowing that he was there, I feared I could not restrain him; thus, I remained silent while suffering inwardly.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported it all to the Buddha.
Thereupon, the Great Sage addressed the bhikṣus:

"This gambler, a man of depraved conduct, has not only in this life used the outward appearance of one who dwells in seclusion out of fear to commit theft and deception; it was likewise so in his previous lives."

The Bhikṣu Upananda did not sever his continuous faith; rather, in the distant past, there was a virtuous man in the city of Rājagṛha who entered the house of a courtesan and, together with that harlot, enjoyed himself with food, drink, song, and dance.
All his wealth and property soon came to an end; his possessions were entirely seized by the courtesan, who no longer permitted him to enter his home.
The courtesan pursued him and repeatedly sent him away, yet he refused to leave.
At that time, the courtesan drove him out of her house; she went away to seek wealth and only returned after doing so.
Failing to obtain wealth, and because of her pursuit of it, she arrived in the land of Uttarakuru.
Although he arrived in that country, he knew nothing of it.
At that time, in the land of Uttarakuru, there was a great householder who possessed abundant wealth and jewels, with immeasurable power and riches.
Feigning benevolence and virtue, he approached the Venerable One and said:

"I am a merchant and a leader of many people. I came from a certain country with a great abundance of wealth and treasures, but on the road I encountered wicked bandits who plundered everything. Having lost all my property and livelihood, I am now impoverished and in dire straits, with no means to sustain myself."
"Having barely obtained enough to sustain my life, I have now exhausted all my strength in running about; I now return to the Venerable One to serve at his side.

At that time, the Venerable One saw her thus, observing her dignified demeanor, her adherence to the rules of conduct, and her measured gait and movements; she possessed majestic spiritual virtue and was truly a noble woman.

I devised a plan to restore it to its former state; that man was clever and wise, possessed of brilliant eloquence, his actions were timely and appropriate, his will was untiring, and his nature was easily awakened; he was most worthy of honor and took delight in himself.

He guards and restrains his mind, never being negligent; he accomplishes all that he undertakes, and there is nothing he does not achieve. His physical conduct is pure, and his speech is gentle, free from any coarseness or harshness.
He was skilled in conversation and eloquent in speech; among all who saw him, there were none who did not rejoice.
His venerable kinsmen and those of his household, both great and small, all held him in deep respect and affection, and they all praised him together.

The Venerable One, seeing this, leaped for joy and comforted him; everyone considered it a cause for celebration. Observing that his conduct was free from any lapse or error, he immediately entrusted him with the mission.
At that time, the Venerable One observed the person’s virtue from both within and without; seeing no flaw or deficiency, he universally encouraged and assisted him, saying:

"In all that this person undertakes, there is achievement. He is foremost in reverence and has never been disrespectful; he is most sincere and faithful, regarding me as a younger brother regards an elder brother, with equal and no distinction."
"His precepts, concentration, tranquility, and discernment are free from deception.
Gradually, he entrusted him with great wealth and assets, which [the son] immediately stole and took outside.
Having loaded his chariot with wealth, treasures, and various fine goods, he returned to the city of Rājagṛha and enjoyed himself in food, drink, and pleasure with a seductive and wanton woman.

At another time, that man did not appear; they searched everywhere for him but could not discover where he had gone. Upon inspecting the treasury, they found that vast amounts of wealth and treasures had been lost beyond measure.
Seeing that he possessed no wealth or treasures, [the man] went everywhere seeking him, but did not know where he had gone. He then heard from others:
"This man has returned to Rājagṛha and is eating and drinking with a courtesan."
"This gambler is no gentleman, nor is he a virtuous man.
The Venerable One thought to himself that as the man had fled far and wide, he could not be recovered; thus, he felt profound resentment.
He uttered this verse in lamentation:
"It is not by being a virtuous gentleman, nor by a handsome and flourishing exterior,
that one can trust a person based on their appearance, nor by their gentle and beautiful speech."
Observe their conduct and actions; though they appear outwardly virtuous, the wise should exercise foresight and test them when living together.
Only then will one know their evil disposition, like the gambler who raised his voice while playing at dice.
I shall not abandon them at that time, for they are like food mixed with poison.
How could one be so ungrateful and likewise callous toward the bonds of affection?
The wise do not associate with such as these; even if they must be saved, they should be abandoned.
"At that time, I happened to see him; out of trust, I was deceived and defrauded.
He was not a worthy man, yet he manifested the appearance of one; he stole my wealth and fled.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“At that time, the Venerable One was this very Bhikṣu Upāli.
The one who deceived him by means of dice was this very son of a gambler who became a śramaṇa and deceived Upāli.”
"In previous lives they encroached upon one another, and in this life it is likewise.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was no one who did not rejoice.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Living by Wrong Means, Number Four. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, Upāli the son of the Śākya clan was preaching the sūtras to people and discussing their livelihoods, speaking only of food, drink, clothing, and bedding.

He preached the sutras for others and lectured on matters of merit and the fruits of karmic retribution, yet he never discussed the wisdom of the Way’s principles; consequently, he obtained a great abundance of robes, bedding, food, drink, and various delicacies.

Having grasped this, they stand apart from the noble ones; there are various matters by which they preach worldly sutras and mundane food and drink, giving rise to all manner of improper discourse, and do not expound the boundless wisdom that transcends the world.

When the bhikṣus saw those who were on their alms-rounds at laypeople's homes discussing only mundane matters such as clothing and food, they immediately rebuked and admonished them, and passed the word along to one another.
When the assembly of students heard this, they immediately followed after him to reprimand and admonish his conduct, saying:

"How can you do this, worthy one? The World-Honored One, the Great Sage, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment through holy penetration, has preached the wondrous Dharma of the world, which is difficult to reach and difficult to comprehend."
The profound and universal Way of the Dao is without thought and without conception; its mind is detached from names, peaceful and free from affliction—the realm realized by the wise.

For incalculable billions of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they have fundamentally followed the various Buddhas, hearing, receiving, and upholding [the teachings], thereby all attaining peaceful and secure deliverance.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they had left their homes out of faith in the household life to pursue the Way, yet they returned instead to recite secular scriptures.

With many thoughts and many desires, they gave rise to various worldly affairs; regarding the food and drink of the mundane world, which are of no benefit to the noble path, they departed from the tracks of the sages and once again discussed secular matters.
Then the bhikṣu went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"This is not a śramaṇa."
"This is not the practice of a fully ordained renunciant; though one lives by the Dharma, one merely seeks food and clothing and has never provided instruction.
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, rebuked him with countless points for having acted contrary to the teachings of the Way and the Dharma.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Upananda, son of the Śākyas, you foolish man!
It is not only in this present life that you have extensively expounded the worldly scriptures for the sake of gain, clothing, and food!"
Desiring to manifest his own fame and cause the multitude to make offerings to him, he was likewise so in previous lives.
In the past, countless eons ago, there was a secluded place where many immortals dwelt.
There was a rishi who was foolish, ignorant, and lacking wisdom; his mind was closed and his intellect obstructed.
For the king’s crown prince and the various ministers and officials, he spoke only of food, drink, various delicacies, and clothing, without discussing the scriptures or the Way.

Knowing the proper time and occasion, he preaches the sutras to those traveling in carriages or on horseback; or he goes to preach the sutras to those who are lost; or he preaches the sutras to those who are obstructed by hindrances; or he praises and preaches the sutras for the sake of food, clothing, and worldly delicacies. It is because of these reasons that he receives exquisite food, drink, and various articles of offering.
At that time, the heterodox brahmins saw this; while they were expounding the scriptures for the prince and the various high ministers, they saw from afar the [prince] riding upon his mount.
Then the seers went to inform their preceptor and the other seers; having heard such news, they all together rebuked and admonished him, saying: "This is not what you should do!"
At that time, the Upādhyāya, a seer possessing the five supernormal powers, questioned the Bodhisattva and immediately rebuked him:
"It should not be thus!
Should anyone commit such an unrighteous act, or should anyone slander it—if one considers these two cases, neither is good."
If one does not regard [the teaching] as marvelous or sublime, yet preaches this sutra for others, they will dwell apart from the noble sages and deviate from the scriptural canons.
As for those who listen and receive it, they likewise ought not to do so; thus, both parties will fall into ruin.
Thereupon, Huinàn (Andhaka) spoke in verse:
"Both parties fail to understand the meaning; In calculating it, both fall into error.
The Dharma is preached without reaching its principle, And the sutra is heard without understanding its significance."
In this mundane world, it is difficult to encounter a divine sage who expounds the principles of the Way;
yet, while providing him with the common fare of food and clothing, the ignorant lament and speak thus:
"He eats only fine rice and is fully supplied with the finest meats."
Relying on the principles of the noble and wise, I wish to discuss and explain the scriptures;
my aspirations lie in dwelling in seclusion, where I subsist on gathered fruits for sustenance.
This is what I admire and delight in—the very dharma praised by the immortals.
Singing the praises of moral tranquility, one becomes a brahmin through the benefit of the Dharma;
with dignified conduct naturally subdued, one should not take pleasure in what is contrary to the Dharma.
Knowing moderation and seeking little, one leaves the home life to practice alms-gathering.
"Better to live by this work than to violate the scriptures.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You who wish to know!"
At that time, he constantly provided clothing, food, and various delicacies while preaching the Dharma, yet did not inquire about the Way; he was none other than the Śākya son Upāli!
Those who purified their Brahma-conduct were the community of bhikṣus present here today;
as for his preceptor, he was I myself, the seer endowed with the five supernatural powers.
"Having met in a previous life, we meet again now.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was no one who did not rejoice.
5. The Buddha Speaks of My Past Experiences. Fifth. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a certain elder of great wealth, possessing immeasurable riches and countless amounts of gold, silver, and precious jewels.

Through diligent toil in their livelihood, they encounter hunger, thirst, cold, and heat; they expose themselves to various hardships and endure the distress of manifold anxieties, accumulating this wealth and enterprise by unrighteous means.

Although they possess wealth, they do not provide for their own food and clothing; they cannot practice generosity; they cannot honor and serve their two parents; and they cannot sufficiently provide for their wives, children, servants, and laborers.
If there is no benefit for one's family, household, or relatives at home or abroad, how can one practice giving to create merit?

One wears coarse clothing, eats poor food, harbors stinginess in one's heart, leaves one's parents in destitution, leaves one's wife and children naked and cold, and does not maintain social relations with those inside or outside the household.
Each followed their own two [paths], constantly fearing disturbance; whatever they sought, they acted with stinginess and greed.
Being so miserly, possessing little merit and no wisdom, they were most anxious and had nothing to bring along.

When he originally engaged in worldly pursuits, he was sometimes sincere and sometimes insincere; he accumulated immeasurable wealth and treasures, yet could not even provide for his own food and clothing.
When his life came to an end, as he had no offspring, all his wealth and treasures were confiscated by the government.
The World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:

"Listen now: suppose a foolish and ignorant man of low station obtains a subtle and exquisite treasure, yet he cannot even provide for his food and clothing, nor does he support his parents, wife, children, slaves, or guests."
"After ten thousand parts have been taken away, there is nothing further to be added, but rather a diminution.
Having heard this, the bhikṣu addressed the Buddha in full detail:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"

There was a householder, named so-and-so, whose wealth was immeasurable; yet he could not provide food or clothing for himself, nor support his parents, wife, children, or servants, nor practice generosity. When his life suddenly came to an end, his property was confiscated by the government.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This venerable elder was not only stingy and greedy, cherishing his wealth and treasures in this present life; it was the same in his previous lives."

In the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a great Gandhamādana Mountain where countless *pippalī* herbs and pepper trees grew. At that time, upon a *pippalī* tree, there lived a bird named "Mine" (*mamaka*) who made his dwelling there.
Suppose that in the spring months, when medicinal fruits ripen, people all gather them to consume as medicine for curing diseases.
At that time, my bird would call out with a mournful cry:
"These fruits are mine; do not take them!"
"My heart does not wish for anyone to pluck me.
As the bird cried out and called, the multitude continued to take [the others], paying no heed to its cries.
That bird, possessing little merit, lamented and wailed with a voice that did not cease; because of this, its life came to an end.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is! Bhikṣu!"

In the meantime, the foolish and ignorant person acts as a lowly official; he travels abroad seeking wealth, whether by righteous or unrighteous means, accumulating riches and treasures. Yet, when his life comes to an end all at once, his wealth cannot accompany him.
It is like that bird named "Mine," who, seeing the *bibhītaka* trees and various medicinal trees about to ripen, cries out and wails piteously: "All these are mine!"
The people then proceeded to gather them, unable to restrain themselves.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“There is a bird named *Mamaka*, Dwelling upon Mount Gandhamādana.”
When the various medicinal trees ripened, the Cakravāka bird cried out, "This is mine!
Hearing that cry of distress, all the other birds gathered together;
when the people took the medicine away, the Cakravāka was filled with grief.
Suppose there were a person who accumulated immeasurable treasures,
yet neither thought of food and drink nor bestowed them upon such birds;
even if faced with officials, thieves, enemies, water, fire, or one's own children, [one would still not give].
They are seized or consumed by fire, just like the medicinal fruits of my teaching.
One cannot enjoy fine food and drink; it is the same with beds and bedding, as well as incense, flowers, and all offerings—all things are like this.
Having already attained this human body and returned to its kind, when life ends it is all abandoned; not a single thing follows the body.
Therefore, one should plant roots of virtue and keep the future world in mind.
The merit performed by a person awaits them in future lives.
Do not let your heart harbor the agony of boiling water and fire when your life comes to an end;
because I previously indulged in negligence, I must now cultivate the roots of virtue.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“If you wish to know, that bird of mine at that time was this very elder here!

Therefore, bhikṣus, you should practice and learn this: one should not be stingy or possessive, but should remove the defiled and turbid mind and always cultivate purity; this is the teaching of all Buddhas!”
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all were filled with joy.
The Sixth Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha: The Quail Sūtra Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a great thicket of trees.
Within that great thicket, a wild cat lived and roamed."

Having fasted for several days, his hunger reached its extreme limit. Upon seeing a wild pheasant atop the king of trees—elegant and beautiful—he cultivated a mind of loving-kindness, feeling compassion for all classes of beings, whether crawling, breathing, or sentient.
At that time, the wild cat harbored a malicious intent and wished to endanger the life of the cock; it slowly approached and stood beneath the tree, speaking in gentle words and reciting this verse:
"Your mind is tranquil and your appearance is extraordinary; you eat fish as if they were fine garments.
Descend from the tree to the ground, and I shall become your wife."
Then the wild cock replied in verse:
“O Benevolent One, you have four legs, while my body has but two.
Considering the nature of birds and wild cats, it is not fitting for us to be husband and wife.”
The wild cat replied in verse:
"I have traveled far and wide, Through kingdoms, cities, towns, and districts;
I desire no other man, For my heart’s delight rests only in you."
Your body appears upright and handsome, your countenance stands foremost in beauty;
I too am subtle and lovely, a girl of pure conduct.
Let us enjoy each other’s company, like a hen roaming outside her coop.
"The two of us share an equal mind; is this not indeed joyful?
At that time, the wild cock replied with a verse: "Do you not know me!"
"Who are you, and what do you seek?
Since your various tasks are not yet fully accomplished, you are not one whom the wise would praise.
The wild cat replied with a verse:
"Having obtained such a wife, One strikes her head instead with a staff;
For those in poverty, this is the height of misery, While for the wealthy, it is like rain falling upon treasure."
"By associating with one's kin, one gains immeasurable great treasures;
by associating with one's family, the mind finds rest and becomes firm.
The partridge replied in verse:
“‘Since you have calmed your mind and followed my instruction, your blue eyes are like a malignant ulcer;
seeing you thus bound in chains, it is as if you were confined within a prison.’”
The Blue-Eyed One replied with a verse:
"You do not share my heart; your words are like thorns.
What will you achieve by this? You shall only bring about sorrow and anxiety."
"My body is neither foul nor filthy; it emits the fragrance of the virtue of precepts.
Why do you wish to abandon me and travel far away to another place?
The wild pheasant replied in verse:
"If you wish to pull it far away, it is as fierce and malevolent as a serpent;
only by rubbing its skin until it becomes soft can you then proceed with your discourse."
The wild cat replied in verse:
"Come quickly down here; I wish to speak with you, and shall also inform my kinsmen and address my parents."
The wild cock replied with a verse:
"I have a young wife, Of upright countenance and virtuous nature;
She observes the precepts with care according to the Dharma, Guarding her mind so as not to transgress."
The wild cat spoke in verse:
"Thus, with thorny staffs, one follows the true teaching while at home;
within the household there are elders, who benefit others through the Dharma and the precepts."
The willow trees stand outside, all flourishing in their proper season;
the multitude together bow their heads to the Benevolent One, as the brahmins serve the sacrificial fire.
My family, by virtue of our power and influence, have served various brahmins.
“May the auspicious one who has many sons cause you to abound in wealth and treasures.
The wild pheasant replied in verse:
“The gods shall grant you your wish; strike him with the Brahma-staff!”
"What dharma exists in this world, by which one might wish to eat chicken?
The wild cat replied in verse:
"I shall not eat meat; I will dwell in the open air and cultivate purity."
"I shall serve the assembly of devas; thus I have obtained this husband!
The wild cock replied with a verse:
"Never before have I seen or heard of such a thing: that a wildcat should practice pure conduct."
"You wish to destroy something; you are a thief who wishes to devour the chicken.
Wood and fruit are distinct things; with your sweet words and feigned laughter, I shall never trust you. How could you fail to devour the chicken?"
Evil-natured and suddenly violent, your face appears as red as blood and your eyes as blue as indigo; you shall eat mice and insects.
You will never obtain chicken to eat—why do you not go out to catch mice?
With a flushed face and eyes starkly blue, you cry out "Cat!"—at which my hair stands on end and I instinctively seek to hide myself.
Life after life I have wished to avoid you; for what reason do you now jostle me?
Then the cat replied with a verse:
"Is your complexion so fine?
Are you all so upright and youthful!"
One should inquire about his majestic deportance and all other meritorious qualities;
how he fulfills all practices, possesses wisdom and skillful means,
and understands the affairs of household life— there has never been anyone equal to me in these respects.
I have always delighted in bathing and grooming; now that I am dressed in fine garments and move with the sounds of dancing and singing, you treat me with such love and respect.
Furthermore, you should wash my noble feet and comb my hair into a topknot for me.
"And once you have been tamed and made playful, only then will you love and respect me.
Thereupon, the wild cock replied with a verse:
"It is not that I do not love myself, that I would let my enemy comb my hair."
"If you remain close to him, you shall never attain a long life.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know, the wild cat of that time was none other than the bhikṣu Cañcā here and now!"
"The cock of that time was my very self!
Our meeting in the past is just like this one now.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was no one who did not rejoice.
7. The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Woman Who Quarreled in a Previous Life. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, Devadatta harbored thoughts of malice in his heart; he slandered the Tathāgata while claiming for himself that he possessed the Way.
The multitude rebuked him, and the devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, and the four heavenly kings, all exhorted him together:
"Do not harbor malice toward the Tathāgata!"
Do not slander the World-Honored One!

The Buddha is the most honored among all those in the three realms; he possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge and is free from all obstructions. From the heavens above to the earth below, there is none who does not take refuge in him.
What is slander? It incurs immeasurable demerit.
For you to wish to disparage the Buddha is like raising one's hand to cast down the sun and moon.
"It is like wishing to leap over Mount Sumeru with a single grain of dust;
it is like attempting to traverse the void with a single hair.
When Devadatta heard this, his mind remained unchanged.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha in full:
"What grave cause for resentment does Devadatta have that he harbors such a deep-seated grudge?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Devadatta was not only like this in this life; it has been so in every lifetime!
Long ago, incalculable kalpas past, there was a brahmin whose wealth was beyond counting.
He had a beautiful daughter, exquisitely fair and of the most excellent appearance.”
According to the law of the brahmins, those of noble lineage should give their daughters to those who are learned in the scriptures.
At that time, the brahmin invited five hundred of his fellow students and provided them with offerings for three months, in order to examine what they knew.

At that time, among the five hundred people, there was one man of supreme wisdom who had studied the three scriptures and was broadly versed in the five canons. He mastered the sequence of chapters and phrases without losing the meaning of the sutras; when questioned, he provided definitive answers without any difficulty or doubt, and thus occupied the position of the foremost elder.
Furthermore, he was aged and decrepit, his facial features were hideous and unlike those of a human, and both his eyes were blue.
His parents were filled with grief and anxiety, and the daughter also harbored distress, thinking:
"How can I become the wife of such a man?"
"How is he any different from a vengeful ghost?
What shall we do about him?

At that time, there was a brahmin from a distant land who was young in years, possessed of exceptionally handsome features, and endowed with intelligence and wisdom. He had mastered the three Vedas and was thoroughly versed in the five classics; he understood celestial phenomena above and observed terrestrial geography below, being able to foresee all portents of calamity and good fortune.

He was able to discern the six types of board games, sorcery, and the arts of bewitchment; he knew how to determine the gender of a fetus and whether childbirth would be easy or difficult. He felt compassion for all beings throughout the ten directions—those that fly and creep, those that crawl and breathe, including the categories of humans and other creatures—and maintained the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
He heard that a wealthy Brahmin of noble lineage had invited five hundred of his fellow students to provide them with offerings for three months, intending to give his daughter to one of them.

He immediately went there and posed difficult questions to each of the Brahmins; they were all brought to exhaustion, unable to offer any response, as the wisdom of the entire group of five hundred fell short of his.

The young brahmin sat in the seat of honor; when the girl’s parents and she saw him, they were all greatly delighted, saying, "We have sought a son-in-law for a very long time, and now our wish has been fulfilled."
The elder brahmin said:
"I am already advanced in years and have long promised my daughter to you as a wife. Let her remain with me for the time being;
whatever gifts or rewards I receive, I shall give them all to you. You may keep this woman, but do not cause me grief by bringing disgrace upon me in my old age."
The youth replied, "One may not transgress the law to follow human sentiment; I ought to take her as my wife, so why would I give her to you?
When the three months had concluded, he gave the maiden to the young brahmin.
The elder among them harbored a heart of malice and said:
"You have insulted and humiliated me and seized my wife; in every life and wherever we may be, I shall remain your enemy."
"Whether it be to cause him harm or to inflict humiliation upon him, he will never let him go.
The young brahmin constantly practiced a mind of loving-kindness, yet he alone harbored malice toward him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the elder brahmin was none other than Devadatta;
the young brahmin was my own self; and the girl was Gopī."
"The karmic bonds of previous lives remain unresolved even now.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was none who did not rejoice.
**The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Lost Pearl Fallen into the Sea, Number Eight.** Thus have I heard: [The Buddha was staying at... (text continues).
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
All were great sages who had already attained mastery of supernatural powers.
At that time, the bhikṣus sat together in the lecture hall and discussed among themselves, saying:

"We [have heard that] for incalculable kalpas, the World-Honored One practiced with diligence and without slackening; disregarding the afflictions of the five realms of birth and death, he sought the Way of the Buddha in order to rescue and deliver all beings."
By means of diligence, he transcended nine kalpas and attained for himself the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, becoming the Most Perfectly Awakened One.
For my sake, he was delivered from suffering and became a bridge for me.
At that time, the Buddha heard from afar the discussion among the bhikṣus; he rose and proceeded to the lecture hall, where he asked them, "What are you discussing?
The bhikṣus replied:

“We have deliberated together and found that the virtues of the World-Honored One are majestic and immeasurable. Since the beginning of countless kalpas, he has practiced with tireless diligence, encountering no hardships and undergoing arduous toil in his quest for the Way. Desiring to deliver all beings, he never fell midway but attained Buddhahood for himself.”
"We have been delivered," they said.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is truly as you have said; it is certainly no different."

Since incalculable kalpas past, I have sought the Way with diligent effort, never succumbing to indolence. Out of compassion for sentient beings, I desired to deliver them; through this diligence, I attained Buddhahood on my own, surpassing nine kalpas and emerging ahead of Maitreya.
I recall that in the past, during incalculable kalpas, I saw that many among the people of my country were impoverished;
I felt compassion and pity for them, wondering by what skillful means I might cause them to become abundant and prosperous.
He thought to himself, "I must enter the sea to obtain the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) in order to bring about salvation.
He beat the drum and rang the bell, crying out, "Who wishes to enter the sea to seek precious treasures?
A great multitude gathered; as they were about to board the ship, he issued further instructions:
"Even if I must abandon my parents and spare no thought for my wife and children, I shall cast myself into the sea and risk my life to enter it together with you. Why is this?
Because the ocean has three perils:
First, there was a great fish twenty-eight thousand *li* long; second, ghosts, spirits, and *rākṣasas* sought to overturn the ship; third, there were mountains being shaken.
For these reasons, he performed this [rite] so that they might be free from resentment.
As soon as the order was issued, the multitude all felt regret.

At that time, five hundred men alone remained firm in their resolve; they hoisted their sails at the mere sight of the wind, boarded their ships, and entered the sea to seek out the Sea Dragon King, requesting from him the wish-fulfilling pearl upon his head.
When the Dragon King saw this, out of compassion for all beings, he exerted himself to enter the sea and, wishing to rescue the destitute man, immediately gave him the pearl.
At that time, the various merchants each gathered treasures until they were fully supplied, and they boarded their ships to return home.
The various nāgas and spirits within the ocean all deliberated together, saying:
"This wish-fulfilling jewel is a supreme treasure of the ocean; it is not something that should be obtained by those of the mundane world."
"How can it be that the ocean is diminished and Jambudvīpa is enriched?
It is truly to be lamented!
We must devise a plan to reclaim its jewel; it must not be lost to the human world."
At that time, the nāgas, spirits, and deities surrounded him day and night for many circuits, desiring to seize his pearl.

Yet the Guide’s virtue was so exalted and his majestic spiritual power so sublime that, although the spirits, nāgas, and deities wished to overturn the ship and take the wish-fulfilling pearl, they were unable to do so by their own strength.
"At that time, the guide and his five hundred followers crossed the sea in safety.
The Bodhisattva leaped for joy and stood upon the shore; bowing his head and lowering his hands, he offered prayers of blessing to the sea deity, while the pearl remained fastened around his neck."
At that time, the Sea Dragon King, seizing an opportunity through his karmic conditions, caused the pearl to fall back into the sea.
The leader was deeply moved and said:

"I traveled into the sea, braving hardships upon my ship with immeasurable toil and suffering, only to obtain this treasure intended to relieve the destitution of the masses; yet now the Sea God has instead caused it to fall into the sea."
He commanded his attendant:
"Bring a vessel; I shall drain the ocean until I reach the mud at its bottom. If I do not find the jewel, I will never rest or grow weary."
He immediately scooped up water with the vessel; through the power of his diligence, undaunted by hardship and disregarding his own life, the water naturally flowed and entered the vessel entirely.
When the nāga deities of the various oceans saw this, fear immediately arose in their hearts:
"The power and vigor of this man's spiritual exertion are truly beyond anything found in the world."
"If we were to squeeze this water now, the ocean would soon be exhausted.
He then brought the jewel and returned it with an apology: "We merely wished to test you;
we did not realize that the power of your diligence was such as this. In all the heavens above and the world below, there is no one who can surpass you, O Guide."

"Having obtained these treasures, I brought them back; the people of the kingdom beheld the treasures and made vows that it might rain the seven precious gems to provide for all under heaven, so that none remained in insecurity or distress.
At that time, the guide was none other than my own self.
The five hundred merchants were these various disciples.
Guided by me, they practiced with diligent energy, entered the great ocean, returned with precious jewels, rescued those who were impoverished, and have now attained Buddhahood.
"Having exhausted the ocean of birth and death, his wisdom is immeasurable; he rescues and delivers all living beings, so that none fail to attain liberation.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was no one who did not rejoice.
9. The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Caṅkī the Violent-Minded Who Slandered the Buddha. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, King Prasenajit invited the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus to take a meal in his inner palace.
The Buddha emerged from the Jeta Grove, surrounded by a great multitude of bhikṣus, as well as bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, and their retinues.
Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings offered worship from above with flowers, incense, and music, sprinkling fragrant liquid upon the ground.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, entered the city of Śrāvastī, intending to proceed to the royal palace.
There was a bhikṣuṇī named Pāpamati who tied a wooden bowl to her belly so that she appeared as if she were pregnant.
She then pulled at the Buddha’s robe, saying:
"You are my husband; since I became pregnant under you, you have provided me with neither food nor clothing—how can this be?"
At that time, the great assembly—the devas, humans, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, gods, ghosts, spirits, and the people of the land—were all struck with alarm, thinking:

"The Buddha is the Honored One of all within the triple world; his mind is purer than a mani jewel, and the brilliance of his wisdom surpasses that of the sun and moon. He walks alone through the three periods of time, and none can equal him."
He subdues all heterodoxies; of the ninety-six kinds, there are none that do not submit.
His virtue and Way are so lofty as to be beyond comparison; like empty space, he is formless and cannot be defiled.
The Buddha’s mind surpasses theirs, and he has no equal.
Since this bhikṣuṇī is already a disciple of the Buddha, why does she harbor such malice, wishing to disparage the Tathāgata?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, perceiving the thoughts of the assembled multitude and wishing to resolve their doubts, looked upward.

At that moment, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, descended immediately and transformed himself into a small mouse. He gnawed the rope binding the executioner, whereupon the executioner fell to the ground. The assembled multitude beheld this; anger and joy mingled within them as they marveled at the cause of what had occurred.
At that time, the king became angry and said:

"This bhikṣuṇī has abandoned her home and distant worldly affairs to become a disciple of the Buddha; yet, instead of being able to eloquently extol the infinite merits of the Tathāgata, she has instead harbored jealousy and slandered the Great Sage!"
He immediately commanded his attendant:
"Dig a deep pit in the ground; I wish to bury him alive!
At that time, the Buddha explained the matter through a parable:
"Do not say such a thing!
This is my own karmic retribution from past lives; it is not solely his misfortune.
Long ago, in a time far distant in the past, there was a merchant who sold fine pearls in great quantities, all of which were perfectly round, brilliant, and beautiful."
At that time, there was a woman who came to purchase it, intending to acquire it for herself.
A man arrived and offered double the price, taking the pearl away alone.
The woman did not obtain it; harboring resentment in her heart, she entreated him again, but he refused to give it back. Her anger mounting, she became enraged:
"Previously, when I was playing with this pearl, you came and seized it from me; yet when I asked for it back, you refused to give it up.

You have brought me disgrace and humiliation; wherever we are born in future lives, I shall repay this enmity to you, bringing you ruin and shame in every place, so that even if you regret it, it will be too late."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus, the king, and the other bhikṣus:
"The man who bought the pearl was none other than myself; the woman was Pāpamati."
"Because of that resentment, in whatever place he is born, he will always seek to slander you.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the doubts of the assembled multitude were resolved, and there was none who did not rejoice.
10. The Sūtra on the Turtle and the Monkey Spoken by the Buddha. The tenth sūtra, "The Sūtra on the Turtle and the Monkey Spoken by the Buddha," was thus heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus gathered together and discussed among themselves, saying:
"There is this bhikṣuṇī, Bhavila, who has abandoned her home and worldly affairs to practice the Way and take refuge in the Triple Gem."
The Buddha is the father;
the Dharma is the mother;
and the assembly of bhikṣus are the brothers.

One becomes a śramaṇa by means of the Dharma; by following and cultivating the principles of the Way, removing the defilements of the three poisons, serving the Buddha-Dharma and the community of bhikṣus, and out of compassion for all beings practicing the four immeasurable minds, one may then attain liberation.
Yet you have instead harbored malice, slandering the Buddha, slandering the Honored One, and disparaging the Sangha; this is most strange and inconceivable, truly unprecedented.
At that time, the Buddha, hearing them from afar, went to ask the bhikṣus:
“What was the subject of your discussion?”
The bhikṣus reported in detail the intent of their discussion.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has not only harbored ill will toward the Tathāgata in this present life; it was likewise so in every place where she was born."

As I recall, in the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a king of monkeys who dwelt among the forest trees, eating fruit and drinking water. He felt compassion for all classes of beings—those that crawl, those that breathe, humans, and non-humans—and desired to deliver them all, leading them to the state of non-action (*anupādāya*).
At that time, he formed a friendship with a turtle; they were affectionate and respectful toward one another, never at odds.
The turtle frequently visited the monkey’s dwelling, where they shared food and drink, conversed, and discussed principles of righteousness and justice.
Seeing that her husband frequently went out and was not at home, his wife suspected he was being licentious and unrestrained with women outside.
She then questioned him, saying:
"My lord, where have you been going so often? Are you perhaps indulging in dissolute and unprincipled behavior abroad?"
Her husband replied:

"I have formed a close friendship with this monkey; he is intelligent and wise, and moreover understands the principles of righteousness. Whenever I go out, I visit him, and we discuss the sutras and the Dharma together. He speaks only of delightful matters and indulges in no other dissipation."
His wife did not believe him and thought it could not be so;
moreover, she became angry,
saying, "The monkey has seduced my husband and caused him to come and go repeatedly."
"I must plot to kill her; only then will my husband rest.
Thereupon, she feigned illness, lying weak and exhausted upon her bed.
Her husband attended to her with great care, providing medical treatment, yet she refused to recover. She said to her husband:
"Why trouble yourself by wasting your medical resources?
My illness is extremely grave; I shall live only if I obtain the liver of a monkey dear to you."
Her husband replied, "This is my close friend;
he has entrusted his person and life to me, and I have never doubted him. Why would I plot against him to use him for your livelihood?"
His wife replied, "Now that we are husband and wife,
sharing one body, it is truly contrary to righteousness and reason that you do not think of supporting me, but instead become like a monkey."
Her husband pressured his wife, who nevertheless held him in high regard.
He went to invite the monkey, saying:
"I have frequently come and gone, stopping at your dwelling; yet you, O benevolent one, have never condescended to visit my door. Now I wish to invite you to my home for a light meal."
The monkey replied, "I dwell on land, while you are in the water; how could we possibly go together?
The turtle answered:
"I shall carry you; you may rely on me.
The monkey followed him, and while being carried halfway along the road, he said to the monkey:
"Do you wish to know why I have come to invite you? My wife is gravely ill and wishes to obtain your liver to consume as medicine so that she may be cured.
The monkey replied, "For what reason did you not tell me sooner?"
"My liver was hanging from a tree; I did not bring it with me.
You must go back quickly to fetch the liver, and only then shall we follow you. He then returned to the tree, leaping and frolicking with joy.
Then the turtle asked, "You were to bring your liver to my home; why instead have you climbed this tree, leaping and bounding about? What purpose does this serve?"
The monkey replied,
"In all the world, none is more foolish than you!
Why do you have a liver that you hang from a tree?"
Having been close friends, entrusting our bodies and lives to one another, you now seek to plot against me and endanger my life; from this day forward, let us each go our separate ways.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the female tortoise was Pāpīyān;
the male tortoise was Devadatta."
"The king of the monkeys was none other than myself.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was no one who did not rejoice.
11. The Sūtra on the Five Rishis Spoken by the Buddha. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and various bodhisattvas.
The Buddha addressed those gathered:
"In the distant past, incalculable kalpas ago, there were five rishis who lived in mountain thickets."
Four served as leaders and one provided service; they made offerings and attended to him without ever failing in their resolve, gathering fruit and drawing water, presenting them at the proper times.
One day they traveled far to gather fruits and water; becoming weary, they fell asleep and failed to return at the proper time.
By midday, the four of them had missed their meal. Gripped by resentment, hunger, and anger, they said to their attendant:
"You who serve us as our attendants—how could you act in such a manner?"
"What you have practiced is fit for malevolent incantations; it is not suitable for one of noble lineage.
Upon hearing this, the attendant was filled with grief beyond words. He withdrew to sit beneath a tree near the water’s edge, sitting with one leg raised, reflecting and reproaching himself:

"I have labored for a long time, yet now I have failed to provide the four seers with their meal at the proper hour. Having lost the Way of the Teacher, I am no longer in accordance with the Four Immeasurables."
Thereupon, he died out of grief.
His feet were always clad in sandals made of the seven treasures; he sat with one foot raised.
While wearing the sandals, he fell into the water, and one sandal was lost.
After his life ended, he was immediately reborn among the non-Buddhists as the son of a malevolent sorcerer.
When he was about ten years old, he was playing with his peers by the side of the road.

At that time, a brahmin passed by and saw the children playing; seeing that their number was quite large, he observed them all thoroughly. Upon seeing the son of the sorcerer, he perceived that he possessed particularly noble marks of one destined to be a king, with a countenance so extraordinary as to be supreme among men.
The brahmin addressed him, saying, "You possess the marks of a king; it is not fitting that you should wander among the crowds in such distress. The youth replied:
"I have cast an evil spell upon you; how can you possess the marks of a king?
The Brahmin replied again, "According to my scriptures, your countenance and physical form accord with the prophetic texts; therefore, you are the one destined by them."
"Reflect deeply upon my words; they are true and without deception.
The king of this country shall pass away on such-and-such a day at such-and-such a time, and he will surely abdicate his throne to you.
The youth replied:
"Please do not spread this far; keep it harmonious, quiet, and secret. If you act according to your words, I shall deeply remember your kindness and dare not be arrogant.
Having finished speaking, the Brahmin immediately fled and escaped to another country.
Not long thereafter, the king passed away without an heir. The ruler sought out a man of virtue to serve as the successor to the state.
The ministers deliberated, saying:
"A state without a sovereign is like a person without a head; we ought to dispatch messengers immediately to diligently seek one of great merit and establish him in his place at once."

The messengers dispersed in the four directions and, seeing from afar that this youth possessed the extraordinary bearing of a transcendent being, immediately sent someone back to inform the ministers:
"Please observe the strict royal protocols and prepare the majestic ceremonial carriage; we pray you come forth to welcome him."
The ministers and officials of all ranks were without exception filled with exultation; as the messenger had reported, they prepared their carriages and went forth to welcome him.

They bathed him in fragrant water and dressed him in the court robes of the five seasons, adorned with a jeweled crown, sword, and sash according to the laws of the former kings, with attendants leading and protecting them before and behind in accordance with national statutes.
Having ascended the throne in the palace and facing south to assume the imperial authority, the realm became peaceful and the common people rejoiced with exuberance.

At that time, a brahmin, observing the celestial phenomena above and examining the terrestrial features below, realized that [the King] had succeeded to the throne; he immediately went to the palace gate to seek an audience.
The gatekeeper reported, saying,
"Outside there is a brahmin who wishes to have an audience with Your Majesty.
The King issued an edict for him to be admitted.
The brahmin entered, performed divinations, offered thanks, and recited blessings; he then addressed the king, saying:
"According to what I have observed, the present result accords with your former vow; is this indeed certain?"
The King said: "How true!
The Way-man is divinely wondrous;
I have received his grace and obtained blessings."
The king said, "O practitioner,
do you perhaps wish for half the kingdom and its hidden treasures?
Women, beautiful maidens, chariots, horses, and attendants— whatever you desire, you shall have!"
The brahmin replied:
"I desire nothing at all, but I seek only two wishes:
first, that in matters of food and drink, movement and rest, clothing and bedding, you treat me as your equal and attend to my needs without distinction of priority; [the second is that... "
"Second, when deliberating on state affairs, one should agree with what is decided and not act with self-will.
The King said, "Excellent!"
"To succeed in these two vows—would this not be easy!
The King governed the state always by means of the True Dharma and did not oppress the myriad people.

Having received the King's favor, the Brahmin became arrogant and self-indulgent, treating the high ministers with contempt. The officials were indignant and resentful, and they all came forward to remonstrate, saying:

"Your Majesty occupies a position of high honor and ought to deliberate with the veteran ministers of the state; yet you have placed exclusive trust in this mendicant, resulting in his negligence and insolence toward the various offices.
When neighboring states hear of this, they will surely mock you, leading to the calamity of invasion."
The King said, "I have long held a fundamental vow with him since our youth; how could I possibly abandon it?
The ministers remonstrated without ceasing:
"If Your Majesty does not require this food for your meal, it shall certainly be changed!
The king then agreed; he waited until the brahmin had gone out, and once the brahmin did not return, he ate the food first.
The brahmin said in anger,
"This was our original agreement.
Why do you eat alone first now?"
The king said, "Although I ate first, you had not yet returned from your excursion; therefore, I prepared a separate meal for you in advance. It was simply that you arrived late.
The brahmin reviled him, saying:
"Alas, you wicked son of a sorcerer! You disregard righteousness and logic, thereby violating your original vow.
When the ministers heard this, they felt that a subordinate was slandering his sovereign; they all petitioned for his execution.
The King issued an edict to his ministers,
asking, "By what crime shall he be punished?
Each of them came forward and said:

"Some say he was steamed in a rice steamer; some say he was boiled; some say his limbs were dismembered; some say he was pounded in a mortar; others say he was killed by being cut five times, having his ears sliced off, his tongue cut out, and his eyes gouged out."
The king had no intention of listening:
"I uphold the Way and its teachings; with a heart of compassion, I take pity on all classes of sentient beings. I do not harm even the crawling insects, much less endanger human life!"
"Simply provide him with provisions and drive him out of the country.
The ministers, obeying the decree, immediately supplied him with clothing and grain and escorted him beyond the borders.
Traveling alone along the distant road, braving both cold and heat, he became utterly exhausted and emaciated, appearing unlike his former self as he reached another kingdom.
He went to the home of a certain brahmin with whom he had long been acquainted, and asked him:
"From where have you come?
What do you study and practice?"
"What sutras did you practice so that you could recite them all from memory? He replied,
"I have come from afar, and being pressed by hunger and cold, I have forgotten what I had studied."
The brahmin thought to himself:
"What this man recites has now been forgotten; he is incapable of teaching others. I shall instead have him work the fields, providing him with a slave boy and oxen for plowing."

He saw a brahmin engaged in the arduous labor of plowing and farming, cruelly ordering his slave boy to level the ground and run back and forth; the slave boy was despondent and wished to throw himself into the water.
When he went to the riverbank, he found a sandal made of the seven precious jewels.
He thought to himself:
"I wish to give this to my master, but my master has shown me no kindness."
"If I wish to give [the sandals] to my parents, I must sell them for food.
This brahmin has oppressed me, making me perform menial labor; I should instead offer them to him, presenting them as wooden clogs, so that I may obtain his leniency and freedom."
He then took the sandals and returned, offering them to the brahmin.
The brahmin was filled with joy and thought to himself:
"The value of these sandals made of the seven treasures is beyond measure."
"I have acted contrary to Your Majesty's will; by offering these wooden clogs to you, my transgressions may be absolved.
He then returned to the kingdom and presented the clogs to the king, deeply confessing his previous faults and offenses, and entreating for pardon and release.
The king said,
"Excellent! He immediately ushered him inside the curtain and seated him on a separate seat.
He assembled his ministers and addressed them, saying:
"Gentlemen, have you not seen the brahmin who was previously expelled? They replied:
“I do not see it. “If one were to see it, what would you do? He replied:
"One should cut off his hands and feet, sever his ears and nose, and decapitate him or cleave his waist; treat him with these five poisons.
The King asked, "If one were to see him, would he be able to recognize him?"
The minister said, "I do not understand!
The king took out his precious sandals and showed them to the assembly of ministers; he then commanded the brahmin to come forth so that he might meet with the minister.
"Since this extraordinary jewel has been brought here, should we not investigate its origins together?
The ministers replied, "The guilt of this brahmin is as vast as a mountain and as deep as the ocean; he cannot be pardoned!"
"I have offered you a single sandal; what can it possibly repair?
If I were to obtain a pair, my transgressions might be expiated!
The king agreed with this and again pursued the brahmin, ordering him to seek out one more sandal.
The brahmin was distressed and thought:
"My original lamentation has only grown more intense.
He returned to his former master, who asked him:
"Where have you come from, and where are you going?
The brahmin concealed himself and did not dare to answer.
When the clouds had passed and it was time to return,
he handed over the oxen and the slave boy to him, instructing him to plow and sow as before.
At that time, the brahmin asked the slave boy:
"Where did you originally obtain those precious sandals?
The slave boy went along with him and showed the place where he had found them; they went to the edge of the water and searched everywhere at their leisure, but could not find a single pair.
The servant abandoned him and departed.
The brahmin thought to himself, "These precious sandals must have come from upstream; if I go downstream to seek them, I shall not find them.
He immediately went against the current, where he saw a great lotus flower being carried by the current and eddying waves, held in the mouth of a fish.
The flower was exceedingly large, with more than a thousand petals.
The Brahmin thought to himself:
"Although I have not obtained the sandals, I shall offer this flower; perhaps I may thus be forgiven for my transgression and restored to former favor."
He then took up the flower again and saw four rishis sitting beneath the trees.
He went before them and paid his respects, inquiring after their well-being and whether their holy bodies were enjoying a myriad blessings.
The seer said: "Indeed! From where have you come?"
He replied, "I have lost the King's favor; though I offered him a single sandal, it was insufficient to expiate my offense. Therefore, I came against the current, seeking it but failing to find it."
The seer replied: "As you are a student, you ought to know when to advance and when to retreat!
That king is our son; we cherish and respect him, sharing with him in eating, sitting, and rising, and attending to his needs."
"How could you suddenly revile me with such malevolent incantations?
Your crime is grave; you shall be executed!
Now, without further questioning, he pointed toward the foot of a tree, saying:

"Furthermore, when the King’s former self was a servant attending upon a rishi, he sat with one leg raised in a fixed posture until his death. His precious sandal fell into the water; while one remained on his foot, he simply took it away for himself."
