The Brahmin took the sandals, prostrated himself to apologize for his transgression, and returned to his own country, where he continued to present them to the king.
The king was immediately filled with joy, the ministers' minds were set at ease, and the Brahmin was restored to his former favor and rank.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The king at that time was none other than myself;
the four rishis were Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and Maitreya Buddha.”
"The brahmin was none other than Devadatta.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, there was no one who did not rejoice.

The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Uncle and Nephew, the Twelfth.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, countless kalpas ago, there were two siblings.
The elder sister had a son who, together with his maternal uncle, served in the imperial workshops weaving gold thread, brocade, silk, and fine gauze—rare and exquisite garments."
Seeing the rare treasures and fine goods within the treasury, their greedy minds were stirred, and they immediately consulted one another, saying:

"We have labored at our weaving with tireless diligence; we know the quality, quantity, and nature of the goods in the various stores. Why should we not take them together for our use to relieve our poverty?"
After nightfall, once the people had settled for the night, he dug an underground tunnel and stole official property in quantities beyond measure.
When the supervisor in charge of the storehouse discovered the next morning that the goods were diminished, he reported the matter to the king.
The King commanded him, saying:
"Do not spread word of this so that outsiders may know it.

To say that the uncle and nephew are thieves implies that the King has many affairs and cannot perceive their deeds; were this to reach later days, they will surely become cowed and fearful, and will certainly return again."
"Furthermore, strictly maintain vigilance and guard the place to await him; should he be caught, seize him and do not let him escape.
Having received this decree, the storekeeper immediately increased the defensive preparations. After a long time, the man returned once more to steal.
The nephew instructed his uncle:
"Uncle, you are advanced in years, frail in body, and lacking in strength; if you are captured by the guards, you will be unable to escape on your own.
Instead, enter the underground tunnel by crawling backward. Should they discover us, my strength is great and I shall rescue and deliver you."
Just as his uncle entered the cave, he was seized by the guards.
As the captors shouted out, the other guards caught the nephew but could not restrain him.
Fearing that they would be recognized the next day, the nephew immediately cut off his uncle’s head, carried it out of the cave, and returned home with it.
At dawn, the Director of the Treasury reported the matter in full to the King.
The King issued another decree, saying:
"Carry out his corpse and place it at a crossroads. Whoever comes forward to wail over the dead body shall be the leader of the bandits."
He cast it away at a crossroads and kept watch over it for many days.

At that time, a great merchant from a distant land arrived, with men, horses, and carriages crowding and choking the road; as they rushed forward and pressed in upon one another, the man was jostled and disturbed, and two carts laden with firewood were driven over his corpse.
The guards reported everything in detail to the king the following morning. The king issued an order to observe closely:
"If your surveillance is not thorough and anyone is found burning [the body], arrest them and bring them here."
Thereupon, the nephew led the young servants to carry torches and perform a dance; the crowd became completely boisterous, and as they threw fire onto the wood, the fuel blazed up fiercely.
The guards were unaware of this and reported everything to the king.
The king issued another decree, saying:
"If the snake has already been tied up, increase the number of guards and keep watch over its bones with strict vigilance. Whoever comes to take the bones shall be the principal culprit."
The nephew also became aware of this; moreover, he secretly brewed wine, specifically making it rich and potent, and went to the guards to sell it in small quantities.
The guards, who had been suffering from hunger and thirst for some time, saw the wine and all bought and drank together. Having drunk too much, they all fell into a drunken sleep.
The captive took the wine jar, received the bones, and departed; the guards did not notice him. At dawn, he reported this again to the king.
The king issued another decree, saying:
"Despite the successive patrols and sentries, we have ultimately failed to capture him. This thief is cunning and sly; we must devise a further stratagem."
The king immediately brought forth his daughter, adorned with necklaces, pearls, and precious ornaments, and established her in a chamber by the side of a great body of water.
A multitude of attendants guarded her, watching for anyone who might approach the girl out of lustful desire.
She had previously instructed her daughter that she might embrace and seize him by surprise, and call out to the crowd so that they could arrest him.

On another night, the nephew secretly came to her; she placed a log in the water and let it drift downstream, shouting and rushing in great haste. The guards, startled, ran toward the sound, crying, "There is a suspicious person!"
He saw only a tree stump, and as it had been for many years, it remained unchanged through repeated observation; the guardian, having grown accustomed to it, slept without alarm.
The nephew then mounted the stump and reached the woman’s chamber; the woman seized his garment, and the nephew said to her, "Why do you pull at my clothes?
You should instead take hold of my arm."

The nephew was naturally wicked and clever; he had previously taken a dead man’s arm to give to the girl. The girl then let go of her garment and instead seized the dead arm, crying out loudly that it was too late.
The guard woke up, and the nephew was able to escape.
At dawn, he reported the matter in full to the king, who again issued a decree, saying:
"This man’s skillful means are peerless and matchless; though we have pursued him for a long time without success, what are we to do?"
The woman then became pregnant and gave birth to a son after ten months.
The boy was exceptionally handsome; she had a wet nurse carry him throughout the kingdom, commanding:
"If anyone sees him and utters a cry of lamentation, bind them and bring them here."
She cradled the child all day long, yet no one offered a word of comfort.

The nephew was working as a baker, staying beneath the baking ovens. When the young child cried from hunger, the wet nurse took the child toward the ovens to buy some cakes for him. Upon seeing the child, the nephew immediately gave him a cake and made a sound to call his attention.
The wet nurse returned and informed the king:
"The child traveled all day long with no one coming near him; when he passed by a bakery, the seller gave him some cakes, and only then did he make a sound."
The king issued another decree, saying,
"Why have you not bound him and sent him here? The nurse replied:
"The child was crying from hunger; the baker gave him a cake, and he cried because of it. He did not suspect him of being a thief—on what grounds was he imprisoned?
The king sent his nurse to carry the child out again, and those who were waiting nearby bound whoever came close to the child and brought them before him.
The nephew purchased fine wine and summoned the wet nurse and the eavesdropper to a tavern.
After encouraging them to drink until they were thoroughly intoxicated and had fallen asleep, he stole the child away.
Realizing they had lost their child, they reported the matter to the king in full detail.
The king issued another decree, saying:
"You all are obstinate and foolish; greedy for the mad water, you have not only failed to catch the thief, but have also lost your child."
The nephew then obtained the child and carried him to another kingdom.

Upon meeting the king, he offered greetings and responded with eloquence, citing scriptures and explaining profound principles. The king was greatly delighted and immediately bestowed upon him a fief and rank, appointing him as a high minister. The king then said to him:
"In my entire kingdom, there is none who equals you in wisdom and skillful means. I wish to give you my daughter, or perhaps one of my own daughters; you may choose whichever you desire."
He replied, "I dare not!
If Your Majesty would show me compassion, the truth is that I wish to seek the daughter of a certain king."
The King said:
"Excellent! Let it be according to your aspiration!"
The king immediately gave him a name and considered him his own son; he dispatched a messenger to go and seek the daughter of that other king, and the king agreed to it.
The king thought to himself:
"This fellow is a persistent master thief, cunning from beginning to end."
He immediately dispatched a messenger, saying:
"I wish to welcome my daughter; send forth your crown prince with five hundred mounted attendants, all of whom must be fully prepared.
The king then issued orders to his outer officials to quickly prepare the chariots and cavalry.
The nephew, being a treacherous minister, was filled with fear and thought to himself:
"If I reach that country, the king will surely discover me and will undoubtedly seize me."
He then addressed the king, saying:

"If Your Majesty would permit me to be sent, I shall dispatch five hundred horsemen, fully equipped with clothing, saddles, and bridles, all identical in every detail; only then may I go to welcome the bride."
The king agreed with his words and immediately went to welcome the bride.
The king ordered his daughter to provide food and drink for the guests and to entertain them well;
two hundred and fifty horsemen preceded her, and two hundred and fifty followed behind.
The nephew was among them, straddling his horse and refusing to dismount.
His father-in-law came out himself and observed him repeatedly.
The King entered the midst of the riders, personally seized the nephew, and brought him out.
"You have employed such skillful means before and after, yet why was he impossible to capture?
He bowed his head and replied, "It is indeed so!"
The King said:
"Your sagacity and wisdom are peerless in all the world; according to your wish, I shall give my daughter to you as a wife, so that you may become husband and wife."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that nephew was at that time, it was I myself;
the king who was the girl's father was Śāriputra."
The maternal uncle was Devadatta;
the father of the king’s wife was Śuddhodana;
and the mother was Māyā.
"The wife was Gopī;
the son was Rāhula. When the Buddha had spoken these words, there were none who did not rejoice.
13. The Discourse on Dwelling in Solitude Spoken by the Buddha. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kuru, accompanied by a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
Upon arriving at a village within the city, there was a natural, exquisite sound, and the Buddha halted therein.
At that time, a brahmin elder from that village, together with an immeasurable multitude, all heard it clearly and universally.
There was one of great and tranquil resolve, surnamed Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan; having renounced his kingdom, he wandered through cities and villages together with five hundred great bhikṣus.
That Buddha, the Great Sage, is renowned far and wide; his fame pervades the ten directions, and there are none who do not proclaim it.

Those who were in doubt are struck with solemn awe and tremble with reverence; all rejoice and revere him, addressing him as Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat.

Thus, out of great compassion, he transforms and enlightens all the Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins in the heavens and among humans, as well as gods and men, by means of the six supernormal powers, walking alone and peerless throughout the three realms.
The Dharma taught in this sutra is good in its beginning, good in its middle, and good in its end.

Its meaning is analyzed with subtle discernment of the truth, purifying the holy life (brahmacarya). To be able to behold such a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is a source of great joy; if one can prostrate and reverently receive the teachings of the Way, the merit and blessings shall be immeasurable.

At that time, the brahmin householder went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. Some respectfully inquired after his well-being and offered thanks; some joined their palms and addressed the Buddha; some greeted him with a bow; some remained silent upon seeing him from afar; and others stood withdrawn to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin householder:
"Suppose someone were to come and ask you: 'Which ascetics should not be supported and served?'"
He replied, "I am unable; only the Buddha may explain it! The Buddha said:

“Should there be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas whose eyes are attached to exquisite forms, whose ears crave the five sounds, whose noses long for fragrant scents, whose mouths dwell upon delicious flavors, and whose bodies rely on smooth textures; whose minds are intent upon various dharmas without relinquishing desire, who harbor greed, envy, and affectionate attachment, and who seek with insatiable intent, burning with the pain of affliction.”
“Such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas as these should not be supported, served, or revered.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If anyone comes to question me, I shall answer them in this way; it accords with the meaning of goodness and is consistent with the transformation of the Dharma.”

Why is this so? Because we are attached to the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, as well as to the attachments of affection; we greedily seek after them without satiety. Such as we are, we are deluded by the five aggregates and bewildered by the six sense-spheres.
Regarding official rank, salary, wealth, and nobility, they do not differ from those of the laity in their lack of diligence;
for this reason, one should not offer worship or show deference to such as these.
The Buddha said to the brahmin householder:
"Suppose someone were to come and ask you: 'Which śramaṇa or brahmin should one serve, honor, revere, and respect?'"
"How should one proceed?
He addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"One who does not cling to thoughts of the five aggregates, the six sense-bases, or lust, anger, and delusion; who practices the renunciation of thoughts regarding forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures—such as these are those who have accumulated merit, who are refined, gentle, and harmonious. It is precisely such individuals as these, the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, whom one should serve."
The Buddha addressed the brahmins and elders of the city and its villages:
"For what reason do you speak these words?
Is there perhaps a comparison [to be made]?"

How could one know that these śramaṇas and brahmins have already abandoned lust, anger, and delusion, and furthermore teach others to abandon attachment to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and endearments, as well as the fever of mental affliction and the insatiability of the various sensory desires?
He replied to the Buddha:

“We have frequently seen śramaṇas and brahmins who were handsome and exceptionally fine, yet they abandoned the desires for forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures; dwelling in seclusion, whether sitting beneath trees, among graves, or in the wilderness, they cast off all faults and evils, their minds seeking nothing, abiding in solitary quietude. They have forever eliminated thoughts regarding the dharmas of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, severing all seeking and contemplating emptiness.”

One should constantly observe such śramaṇas and brahmins who have abandoned lust, anger, and delusion, and who also teach others to abandon them; who have relinquished thoughts of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects;
who, having heard this, take it as their joy, and have forever eradicated all attachment to affectionate love.

When one has suddenly and completely detached from all desirable forms and objects of longing that are sought after, then even the seasonal offerings of what is enjoyed—the five aggregates and the six sense organs—are likewise treated in this manner.

I observe these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas dwelling in seclusion—whether sitting beneath trees, among burial mounds, or in the wilderness—abiding alone in quietude, having forever eliminated [the attachment to] forms for the eye, sounds for the ear, fragrances for the nose, flavors for the tongue, tangibles for the body, and mental phenomena for the mind; they have accumulated the roots of manifold virtues and are reverent, compliant, harmonious, and elegant. It is such as these that we observe.

“Śramaṇas and brahmins who have abandoned lust, anger, and delusion, as well as those who teach others to abandon them—to these we today take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; we accept the five precepts and become lay followers.”

The Fourteenth Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha: The Parinirvāṇa of Śāriputra. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa, the Bamboo Grove.

At that time, Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa. His attendant Cunda made offerings and served him according to the Dharma until all was complete; he then took the bowl and robes and proceeded to Rājagṛha.

"Indeed, O Venerable One!"
"Do you wish to know?

"And bring along his robes, bowl, and relics.
The Buddha said to the venerable Ānanda:

"In your mind, do you think that the bhikṣu Śāriputra has entered parinirvāṇa while still possessing the aggregate of morality, or has he entered parinirvāṇa while still possessing the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation?"
Furthermore, having realized this Dharma and attained supreme perfect enlightenment, I have analyzed and expounded it;

as well as the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path—all of which are the manifestations of the Buddha’s faith.
"You now see that the bhikṣu Śāriputra has entered parinirvāṇa, yet you instead grieve and lament, weeping with sorrow and unable to restrain yourself.
The Worthy One addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The bhikṣu Śāriputra has not entered extinction while carrying away the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation."
The World-Honored One has distinguished these dharmas in order to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment and has merely explained them through such distinctions!

Furthermore, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—He does not bring these along when He enters parinirvāṇa!
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!

The bhikṣu Śāriputra upholds the true reality of the precepts and possesses wondrous eloquence. He expounds the Dharma without weariness, and the fourfold assembly listens to him without fatigue. He teaches tirelessly, providing much encouragement and assistance; he transforms those who do not yet understand, causing their hearts to rejoice, such that none fail to receive his instructions.”

Knowing moderation and contentment, he is constantly resolved upon diligence; his will is always settled and stilled. Possessing the great sage’s wisdom and boundless insight, when suddenly questioned, his words respond to the occasion and are dispatched forth. Broadly erudite and capable of full comprehension, he answers immediately upon hearing a sound; he can penetrate all things, taking wisdom as his treasure and being fully endowed with all virtues.
The Bhikṣu Śāriputra was so sublime and majestic.
Therefore, seeing the Bhikṣu Śāriputra depart into parinirvāṇa, I am filled with grief and sorrow; my heart is overcome with such profound lamentation that I cannot bear it myself!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"For one born into this world, how can they remain for long?

All phenomena that arise through the conditioning of mental formations must inevitably reach their end; they perish and vanish forever. Such is the nature of things to collapse; such is the nature of things to decay."
"If one wishes it were not so, it can never be obtained.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The Buddha has always said himself that all those bound by affection must inevitably part."

Now, life has its end; things that have come into being inevitably decay; what is joined must eventually disperse. Since it is the natural law that all things must perish and fall into ruin, how can one’s desires be fulfilled if one wishes them to be otherwise?
"One must eventually pass away and return to impermanence; since this is the law of separation, how could one possibly achieve a state where there is no parting?
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Wherever Śāriputra dwells, my mind is at peace, and I have no cause for concern."
One must inevitably part; all things are subject to decay and impermanence. How could one possibly prevent this? Phenomena arise and then cease;
things are formed and then destroyed; human life has its end; prosperity must inevitably decline—all these are the nature of impermanence.
The law of separation cannot be avoided; it is impossible to prevent it from occurring!
It is like a mountain of great jewels, whose lofty summit suddenly collapses.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
The bhikṣu Śāriputra, who was among the assembly of monks, has now entered parinirvāṇa like the collapse of a mountain of jewels.
Impermanence brings about ruin and destruction; this is the law of separation. How could one wish that it never come to pass and yet have it happen as one desires?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"It is like a great jewel tree, whose roots, sprouts, trunk, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all fully developed and lush; yet if a large branch suddenly falls off, it appears diminished, and when looked upon, it lacks majesty."
Thus it is, Ānanda!
While the bhikṣu Śāriputra was present among the Saṃgha, now that he has attained parinirvāṇa, the majesty of the Saṃgha has diminished; it should utterly perish.
Impermanence and decay are inevitable; how could one possibly prevent them from occurring?
Therefore, Ānanda, from this day forward, cultivate your own bodily conduct, seek refuge in yourself, take the Dharma as your witness, and take refuge in the scriptures—do not seek any other refuge.
How does a bhikṣu practice in this way?

Herein, a bhikṣu observes his own bodily conduct, both internally and externally, as not-self; he should thus examine himself, discipline his mind, and observe that all worlds arise from a lack of wisdom.
Contemplating internal sensations and contemplating external sensations, one realizes that both the internal and external are not-self; thus entering into "Excellent!

One disciplines the mind and examines the ignorance of the world; contemplating the internal mind and also contemplating the external mind, one finds neither internal nor external; thus entering into "Excellent!"

He disciplines his own mind, observing that the world lacks wisdom; he observes the sun and moon above, and likewise observes external phenomena; not relying on either the internal or the external, he enters into the state of "Excellent! (Sādhu).
"Subdue your mind and contemplate that the world lacks wisdom.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This is what it means to cultivate bodily conduct, to seek refuge for oneself, to abide in the ground of the Dharma, and to take refuge in the Dharma alone—not abiding in another ground, nor taking refuge in any other person."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who receive my teachings shall cultivate themselves, seek refuge for themselves, abide in the ground of the Dharma, and take refuge in the ground of the Dharma; they shall take refuge in the Dharma alone, not abiding in other grounds nor seeking refuge in others."
"A bhikṣu who has left the household life is a disciple of the Buddha; one who accords with this teaching accords with the Buddha's teaching.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, Ānanda, the śrāmaṇeras, and the assembly of bhikṣus rejoiced upon hearing the sutra and withdrew, having received his instruction.
15. The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Death of a Son. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a certain man whose son had passed away.
His parents held him in such deep affection that they could never look upon him enough; their longing for him knew no satiety.

Because of my anxiety for you, I have become deranged and lost my composure; I have run through the gates, courtyards, and streets seeking you, wishing that you would come to see me—where indeed might I behold your form?
At that time, the man followed the path out of Śrāvastī, went to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, and approached the Buddha, standing silently before him.
The Buddha asked the man:
"For what reason did you formerly restrain your mind, yet now your faculties have become disordered and unstable, and you are so withered and utterly exhausted?
The man addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Why do you ask me about the transformation of my faculties?
For what reason? I have an only son whom the whole family holds dear; there is no one who does not revere and love him, gazing upon him without ever being satiated."
Now that my life has passed away, I have gone mad out of grief for you;
my mind is deluded and confused, so I open the windows and doors to search for you, wishing that you would come to see me. Why do you seek a son?
The Buddha said:

"When a person is deeply attached to the bonds of affection, separation brings sorrow; they weep and lament, suffering the affliction of grief and distress. Where there is meeting, there must be parting; whatever one loves will inevitably lead to suffering and affliction."

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the man suddenly realized in his heart that the world is impermanent and that the three periods of time are like an illusion; he immediately received the Buddha’s precepts, prostrated himself, and withdrew.

The worthy Revata immediately went to where Śāriputra was, carrying a cooling fan in his hand as he approached him. Why was this?
Today, we shall hear the preaching of the Dharma through Śāriputra, with all the great disciples of one mind.

You have been able to humble yourself to serve as the Buddha’s attendant, drawing near to the World-Honored One to proclaim his holy and enlightened teachings.
You should now question Ānanda regarding the doubts that arise in your mind!
The groves of trees with their melodic sounds provide its music;

"How does a bhikṣu manifest noble virtue while staying among the grove of Sound Trees?

Śāriputra asked Mahākāśyapa, "What do you think?
Is it pleasant to dwell among the grove of trees known as Sound?"
His majestic spiritual power is towering and sublime; his flowers and fruits are lush and abundant; their fragrance is sweet and pervasive, and they are soft and pleasing to people.
How does a bhikṣu manifest noble virtue while dwelling among the grove of trees of sound?
Kāśyapa replied: "Indeed, Śāriputra!
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who dwells in seclusion himself and encourages others to dwell in seclusion;..."
They cultivate the noble and holy themselves and encourage others to do so;
they wear coarse clothing themselves and encourage others to do so;
they know contentment and moderation themselves and encourage others to do so.
One seeks little for oneself and encourages others to seek little;
one is tranquil oneself and encourages others to be tranquil;
one is diligent oneself and encourages others to be diligent.
One restrains one's own mind and encourages others to restrain their minds;
one stabilizes one's own mind and encourages others to stabilize their minds;

when a bhikṣu is amidst the grove of trees of sound, he manifests wondrous elegance.

"How does a bhikṣu, while dwelling among the grove of sounds, manifest noble virtue?

In the manifestation of transformations, he displays infinite forms; he can transform a single body into an incalculable number and then return it to oneness.
He passes through walls, mountains, thickets, and valleys without obstruction; he emerges from the solid and enters the seamless;

emitting flames from the body, like a great mass of fire.

"How does a bhikṣu manifest noble virtue while dwelling among the groves of sound?

excellent, Revata!

Excellent, excellent, Aniruddha! What you have said is well spoken.

Excellent, excellent!

"You have seen the Four Noble Truths and no longer harbor any doubt. Excellent,

Listen further to my words:

His majestic spiritual power is towering and sublime; his flowers and fruits are lush and abundant. His fragrance is sweet and pervasive, and his form is supple and pleasing to the people.

Thereupon, at dawn, the bhikṣu takes his robes and bowl and enters a village; if he is in a foreign land, he stays beneath a tree.

"Only when my own body has exhausted its outflows and my mind is liberated shall I rise from this seat.

Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Extensive learning and upholding the Dharma are most subtle and supreme; Discerning the sūtras and understanding the meaning of the Dharma,"
He preaches for the sake of those who are infinite in number; his mind is set on dwelling in seclusion and delighting in solitude.
Internally observing his own body and externally exhorting others to transformation, he governs himself with joy in dhyāna and practices it within his own person.

Contented, liberated, and teaching according to the capacities of beings— Such are the virtues of one who abides in a quiet retreat.
Whether in the heavens or the Brahma palaces, whether among the gandharvas or in the human realm, he can reach them all without obstruction;
such is the virtue of one who dwells beneath the *yan* tree.

The Seventeenth Sutra Spoken by the Buddha: The Impermanence of Kātyāyana. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Āhuti.
At that time, the Venerable Kātyāyana addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen, worthy ones!
All that is joined together must inevitably be separated."
Though one may enjoy peace and security, illness will inevitably arrive; though young, one must grow old;
though long-lived, one must eventually return to death, like a flower of the morning dew that falls as soon as the sun rises.
The impermanence of the world is likewise so.
Youth and vigor cannot endure forever;
they are like the rising sun that shines upon the world but soon sets.
Thus it is, worthy one!
Gatherings must end in parting; human life ends in death; prosperity inevitably declines. All things in the universe return to impermanence, meeting with ruin and ending in extinction.
Just as when the fruit of a tree ripens, it soon faces the sorrow of falling;
so too are all things impermanent.
Where there is meeting, there must be parting; that which rises must inevitably decline.
For example, just as when a potter makes various earthenware vessels—whether unbaked or baked—all are subject to breaking and decay.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of these bodhisattvas—that the seated bodhisattvas wished to question the Tathāgata regarding the state where Buddhas have no fixed location yet nowhere do they not abide—[spoke as follows].

"The majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas and their universal radiance, the meritorious virtue of the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, and their peerless diligence, have all been established and have entered into the dhāraṇīs and the vast, holy awakening of all Buddhas."
The entry into these states is so extraordinary that there is no obstruction; the entry of the body is likewise in every respect thus.
The retinues of all Buddhas have cast off all defects; the Dharma of all Buddhas cannot be grasped, yet it is ever peaceful and secure.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha entered the mind that accords with the destination of all phenomena; he was without obstruction, and the Dharma-gates he contemplated were free from all defects and hindrances.

The practices of all bodhisattvas consist of the vows of Samantabhadra; they gather these equal practices, abide correctly in their vows, enter into all Buddha-dharmas, behold the Buddhas of the ten directions, bestow great compassion, deliver beings to the infinite, subdue sentient beings, and bring rest to the evil realms.

All the samādhis and meditative concentrations of the bodhisattvas perceive the primordial limit; the wisdom of all Buddhas is inexhaustible in its practice, such that there is none who does not submit to it. They proceed toward the wisdom of all paths, universally illuminating the treasury of the lotus—the dhāraṇīs and the discernment of the various perfections.
Those bodhisattvas, receiving the holy command of the Buddha, each spoke, saying:
"May all Buddhas listen!

The practices of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are immeasurable; their great transformations are supreme. In accordance with their fundamental characteristics, they clearly understand all phenomena and know them all. The Buddhas are transcendent and extraordinary, entirely free from the hindrances of the aggregates."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, universally reach the Dharma-realm and enter the Dharma-realm; throughout all Buddha-worlds, they have no fixed location and encounter no obstruction.
What are the ten?
While in the Tuṣita Heaven, he manifests the exhaustion of his lifespan and suddenly vanishes; there is nothing that can restrain him, nor is there any place where he remains.
He enters his mother’s womb and is born after ten months.
Furthermore, having renounced his home and delighted in departing for the outside world, his mind was constantly joyful.
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, he accumulated all the teachings of the Buddhas.
In a single moment, throughout all Buddha-lands, he manifested the auspicious responses that move the Tathāgatas.
They constantly turn the wheel of Dharma, planting all roots of virtue and providing detailed explanations.
When they attain Buddhahood, they will fully become Bodhisattvas, perfected through the Dharma.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have no permanent dwelling place; wherever wisdom is established, they abide there.
Thus, O Son of the Buddha, they have no location and no place of residence.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
All World-Honored Ones have ten categories of teaching.
What are these ten?
To transform and edify all beings through the various perfections (pāramitās), to eliminate all dharmas of ignorance, and to constantly cultivate great compassion;

to possess the ten powers (daśabala); to universally turn the wheel of Dharma, to transform the multitudes, to restrain sentient beings, to achieve equal enlightenment, to open the way for all sprouts of life, to cause them to have no place of abiding, to take refuge in this dharma of signless non-action, and having attained tranquility oneself, to also teach others to reach the awakening of nirvana—these are the ten.
"Furthermore, Sons of the Buddha!
There are another ten matters by which one may swiftly behold the Tathāgata.
What are these ten?
Upon seeing the various Buddhas, one perceives sentient beings and immediately abandons all points of attachment.
To state the essential point: one swiftly becomes fully endowed with a retinue of merit, quickly receives the roots of all virtues, and thereby attains purity.

Being free from any deficiency, they immediately eliminate their doubts; upon seeing the various Buddhas, who manifest the Mahāyāna for the sake of all sentient beings and cause them to be without fear, they quickly attain accomplishment and become non-retrogressive.

Having now had the good fortune to behold the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, one should swiftly seek to discern the source of sentient beings and bring them across; thus, one shall attain the transcendence of the world and purify the faculties of all beings.
"Whenever one succeeds in beholding the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, there will be no further obstructions or hindrances.
This constitutes the tenth.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bodhisattvas rejoiced upon hearing the sutra.
23. The Sūtra on the Explanation of What is Delightful, Spoken by the Buddha. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

The disciples of Śākyamuni whom he delighted in were numerous; they traveled far and wide, coming and going without restraint, visiting clans and families beyond all counting—sometimes by dawn, sometimes at dusk, and sometimes entering early and departing at nightfall.
At that time, Ānanda, Udāyin, Bakula, and others gathered together in one place and said to the son of the Śākyas whom they admired:
"Venerable sir!
Why do you come and go so frequently without regard for the proper time? Why do you enter and leave at inappropriate moments?"
"Wherever one goes, how can one not exercise self-restraint?
Upon hearing this, the delighted Śākyaputra immediately reviled Saṃgharakṣita, uttering harsh and coarse words:
"You all are ignorant, causing a restless commotion; you cannot find peace for yourselves, shouting and using foul language."
"You all are indolent and do nothing to establish or maintain anything for the Sangha.
Whenever I go out or come in, I must always personally prepare what is required for the Sangha.
Are you able to bear such toil?"
"Have you prepared anything for the assembly of monks?
Do not say of me: 'He has many affairs to attend to.'"
"Virtuous ones, your many duties are even greater than my own.
The delighted Śākyaputra said:
"You gentlemen still have other matters to attend to; how do you think you compare to me in managing the affairs of the Saṃgha?"
At that time, the bhikṣus all made the same resolve.
Then those three men spoke with gentle words:
"His majestic virtue is exceptionally sublime; by relying on his original meritorious conduct, he has achieved much more than they have, surpassing them all."
The beloved son of the Śākyas said:
"This dull and foolish man, with his impetuous resolve and ignorant self-reliance, has forcibly sought what he desired, yet he did not obtain it according to his will."
A certain deva went to the house of a householder and obtained a large jar full of various offerings.
The Venerable Ānanda went to another householder and, with gentle words and firm virtue, preached the Dharma for him, causing his family members to rejoice and leap for joy.
Having attained the status of a *bhikṣu*, he received great offerings; whatever was bestowed according to his wishes, he neither coerced nor solicited.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, recounting the matter from beginning to end.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Regarding these four people, it is not only in this present life that they have quarreled over the merit of their alms-round; rather, there was only one person who obtained meager gains, while the others received much."
Ānanda, the bhikṣu was encouraged and supported by the multitude, finding peace in all things.
In the distant past, at a time beyond reckoning, in another land, there were four men who were close friends; they gathered together and dwelt in one place.
At that time, there was a hunter who, having hunted and caught a deer, was about to enter the city.
They consulted one another, saying:
"Let us devise a plan to follow this hunter and demand the venison; we shall see who has obtained the most."
They set out together immediately; one of them spoke these words, uttering coarse speech and holding himself in high esteem:
"Hey, you man! You ought to grant me your flesh, for I wish to eat it."
The second man said, "Brother,
please give me your flesh so that your younger brother may have food.
The third man said:
"The benevolent one is so dear that he has given me his flesh; I long to eat it.
The fourth man said, "He gave his flesh out of deep affection and offered it as a gift; I wish to eat it."
"All were hungry and thirsty.
Then the hunter observed the words of the four men; according to what each had said, he replied with a verse:
'Your speech is exceedingly coarse; how could I give you meat? "
"His words are like thorns piercing a person, yet he merely offers them his horns.
He then replied to the second man with a verse:
"This man is most virtuous!"
"Thinking of me as his elder brother, his words were like those for one's own limbs; he then took one of his feet and gave it to me.
Furthermore, the third person replied with a verse:
"He gave to me what is lovely and worthy of respect, his heart filled with compassion."
"His words were like those from one's own belly and heart; he immediately gave him his heart and liver.
Furthermore, the fourth person replied with a verse:
"Because you treated me as a close friend, my body attained a bond of common purpose."
"This is truly excellent! Since you are willing to give away all your flesh, I shall grant you your wish.
At that time, the hunter, according to their respective aspirations and whether their speech was coarse or refined, gave each of them a portion of his flesh.
At that time, a deity spoke in verse:
"The words of all men become gentle and return to one's own person;
therefore, do not speak harshly, for neither misfortune nor benefit ever leaves the body."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The first of those who use coarse speech is the son of the Śākyas whom I delight in; the second is Udāyin; the third is Kālodayin; and the fourth is Ānanda!"
"The one who spoke the verse was none other than my own self.
Our meeting at that time is just like our meeting now.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was no one who did not rejoice.
24. The Sūtra on the Five Men Spoken by the Buddha Regarding the King. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the venerable bhikṣus each gave rise to this thought and said:

"The worthy Śāriputra, the worthy Aniruddha, the worthy Ānanda, Śūḍodana, and their five hundred disciples were all at one time together in renouncing the household life to follow the Way. Free from longing or attachment, and with no ambition for worldly glory, they have all become śramaṇas."

At that time, Śāriputra was praised as the foremost in wisdom; he severed the doubts of the multitude, mediated disputes, and discerned the principles of the Way, being unimpeded in all things, like a torch in the darkness that illuminates much.

At that time, Aniruddha marveled at his skillful ingenuity; as a master craftsman for the multitude, he accomplished many things and displayed various arts that brought joy to people, being foremost in craftsmanship.

At that time, Ānanda marveled at his supreme physical beauty and form; his countenance was so exquisite that all who saw him were filled with joy. He was beloved and esteemed by all, and everyone revered him, praising him as a Buddha endowed with the thirty-two marks.

At that time, Śūradatta practiced with such diligence that he never grew weary; his energy was so peerless in the world that it was worthy of praise, and he was further able to enter the ocean and accomplish many things.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, was born into the Śākya clan; he renounced his kingdom and abdicated his kingship to attain the Way of the Buddha, becoming peerless in his upright beauty and foremost in his physical form.

Like the moon among the stars, his radiance surpasses that of the sun; his body is sixteen feet tall, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. His voice, reaching the eight classes of beings, produces ten trillion sounds; the Dharma he preaches brings liberation and understanding to each, so that gods, dragons, spirits, ghosts, and all categories of humans and non-humans each attain their proper place.
The Buddha’s brothers, nephews, and grandnephews, though each praised their own merits, all took refuge in the Buddha and became his disciples.
The Buddha’s virtues are beyond measure; having accumulated merit over countless hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, he attained Buddhahood by himself and now reveals the path to all people.
They went together to visit the Buddha and asked:
"Regarding their origins and backgrounds, who is the foremost?
When we gathered together, each of us praised his own particular strengths."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“These people not only praise themselves and constantly extol their own superiority as peerless in this present life, but it was likewise so in previous lives. In every birth to which they have returned, they have all submitted to my domain; my honor is infinite.”

Why is this? In the past, incalculably long ago, there was a king named Mahānāva (Great Ship). His kingdom was vast and expansive, fully endowed with a multitude of officials and ministers; the land was fertile and prosperous, and its population was flourishing.
The king had five sons:
the first was Wisdom, the second Skillful Artistry, the third Handsomeness, the fourth Diligence, and the fifth Merit; each of them praised his own particular excellence.
That one of wisdom sighed in praise, declaring that his wisdom was the foremost in the world, and spoke in verse:
"Wisdom is the most supreme; It can resolve all doubts and delusions.
It discerns meanings difficult to understand, And reconciles long-standing knots of enmity."
"By means of skillful expedients, he enables people to find their proper place;
when the masses behold this, they rejoice and all together offer equal praise.
Second, he praised his craftsmanship, speaking in verse:
“The artisan possesses skill and technique, capable of accomplishing much;
he constructs a wooden figure by means of mechanical devices, making it look exactly like a human form.”
"In every movement and gesture, whether bending or stretching, there is no observer who does not rejoice;
all together they offer him gifts, for his skill may be relied upon.
The third person, sighing in admiration of his comeliness, spoke in verse:
"Most excellent in comeliness, his physical form beyond compare;
as the multitude beholds his countenance, there is none far or near who has not heard of him."
"All come to revere him; he attends to his duties with universal diligence.
His family serves him as if he were heaven, like the sun emerging from the clouds.
The fourth person, sighing in praise of his vigor, spoke in verse:
“Vigor is foremost; by entering the great ocean through vigor, one can transcend all hardships and calamities and acquire abundant treasures and wealth.”
"Brave, versatile, and capable, Because of this, he meets no obstruction;
All his household affairs are successfully accomplished, And his kinsmen revere and cherish him.
The fifth person, praising merit, spoke in verse:
“Merit is foremost; wherever one goes, things arise spontaneously.
Wealth and joy are without limit, and in birth after birth, one becomes a field of merit.”
“Puṇya shall become Śakra, Lord of the Devas; he shall become a Brahmā or a Cakravartin King, and he shall also attain the Way of the Buddha, becoming fully endowed as a Dharma-King.
Thus each spoke of his own excellence, each claiming to be the foremost, yet none could decide between them.
Each formed his own resolve and would not yield to the others, saying to one another:

"We shall each test our own merit and manifest the marks of a great man by traveling far to various kingdoms and visiting other lands; only then shall we distinguish who possesses superior virtues and who is the foremost!"
At that time, the wise one enters another kingdom and inquires after the virtues and vices of its people,
whether grain is expensive or cheap,
and who among them are wealthy or lowly.

He heard that in his kingdom there were two elders whose wealth was unrivaled and who had long been close relatives; however, they had become estranged from one another, and through the instigation of crafty people, they had fought until they harbored mutual resentment. Years had passed, yet no one had been able to reconcile them.
That wise man, employing skillful means, brought various excellent gifts and a hundred kinds of food and drink, and went to the elder’s gate seeking an audience.
The elder saw him immediately.
He presented the gifts he had brought and, addressing him by his name, offered his apologies and inquiries:

"Previously, we became estranged because my intentions were insufficient and the people around me fostered deceit, resulting in a knot of resentment. For many years we have been separated, unable to meet and converse."

Reflecting on the hardships of serving him face-to-face, I have sent these gifts of food and drink; I hope you will accept them without reproach. Furthermore, as there is neither resentment toward my father nor enmity toward my mother, I have sent me here to convey my intentions to you.
Upon hearing this, the elder was filled with joy and delight, saying:
"I have long desired reconciliation!

However, as there was no kinsman to convey my intentions, you have instead condescended to send a letter and trouble yourself to come and speak with me; this is truly more than I could have hoped for."
"Accepting your kind intention, I shall comply with your instructions and dare not disobey your command.
The wise man understood the elder’s meaning; his doubts were instantly dispelled, and he took his leave and withdrew.

He went to the second elder and did exactly the same; he explained the matter to him as previously described, and they immediately set a date to meet at a certain place, where they gathered the people together to reconcile their enmity.

They feasted and drank at the appropriate time, performing various musical entertainments and enjoying themselves together. Each asked about the origins of the conflict and expressed their intent for reconciliation; they then realized that this man, through skillful means (*upāya*), had reconciled two enemies and restored them to their former intimacy.

Each thought to himself: "We have long been estranged, and though we are all people of this same kingdom, we were unable to reconcile. Yet this man has come from afar to inform us and bring about our reconciliation; his kindness is immeasurable and cannot be fully expressed in words."
Each offered him one hundred thousand taels of gold as a gift!
Taking these treasures, he gave them to his brothers and spoke in verse:
"Endowed with perfect speech, His eloquence can compose the scriptures."
The true person who is able to hear extensively attains peace and security to the ultimate end.
Behold me through wisdom: I have acquired these various treasures, and my food, clothing, and other necessities are fully provided, as well as those given in charity to others.
“At that time, the second artisan traveled on to another country.

At that moment, the king, who delighted in various arts and crafts, had a mechanical wooden man constructed from timber. Its appearance was upright and handsome, no different from a living person; its clothing and complexion were peerless, and it was exceptionally clever. It was skilled in song and dance, its movements were like those of a human, and it spoke these words:
‘My son has been born for so many years; he is honored by the kingdom and receives many gifts.’”
Upon hearing this, the king ordered an artisan to perform a feat; the king and his consort ascended the pavilion to observe.
The artisan’s singing, dancing, and various maneuvers, as well as his prostrations and movements, surpassed those of a living human being.
The king and his consort were filled with immeasurable joy.
He then cast a sidelong glance at the consort with a lustful look.
When the king saw this from afar, he was seized with indignation and urgently commanded his attendants:
"Bring his head here!
Why did you glare at my lady with such malevolent intent?
Your gaze was suspicious and full of ill will."
The father wept, shedding five streams of tears, and kneeling with bated breath, he pleaded for his life:

"I have but one son, whom I love most dearly; whether sitting or rising, advancing or retreating, he was my solace against sorrow and anxiety. It was merely that my foolish mind failed me, resulting in this transgression."
"Even if I were to kill him, I would die with him; I only beg you to show compassion and pardon his transgression.
At that time, the king was filled with such intense rage that he refused to listen.
He spoke again to the king, saying:
"If I am not to live, I pray that you kill me with your own hand and not let another do so.
The king then granted his request.
He then pulled out a wedge from one shoulder, whereupon the mechanical joints fell apart and were shattered upon the ground.
The King was struck with amazement and cried,
"How could my body have ever felt anger toward a piece of wood?"
"This artisan's skill is peerless in the world; the construction of this mechanical device with its three hundred and sixty joints surpasses that of a living person!
He then bestowed upon him a reward of one billion taels of gold.
He immediately took gold and gave it to his brothers, providing them with food and drink, and spoke in verse:
"Behold this master craftsman, Who has achieved so much;
This wooden man made by mechanical means Surpasses those born of flesh."
“Performing songs and dances with instrumental music, we have caused the Venerable One to rejoice;
having received various jewels as a reward, who among us is the most excellent?
Thus spoke the third beautiful woman, as she departed for another land.

When the people heard that one of upright appearance had come from afar—one whose physical form was foremost and rare in the world—they all went out to welcome him, offering him food and drink of a hundred flavors, as well as gold, silver, and precious jewels as gifts.

That man performed his artistry, and the multitude was all the more delighted; they gazed upon his radiant countenance as if upon the moon among the stars. A daughter of noble and wealthy family, possessing vast treasures and overflowing storehouses, presented him with countless billions of rare and extraordinary jewels.
Having obtained this treasure, she spoke these verses to her brothers:
“Excellent! Your complexion is like a flower, Your countenance is perfectly beautiful;
You are respected by women, And you shall always enjoy peace and security.”
"Observed by the multitude, he is like the moon among the stars;
now having acquired various jewels, he consumes them himself and bestows them upon others.
The fourth person of diligence then departed for another country.
Arriving at the bank of a river, he saw a sandalwood tree being carried downstream by the current. He stripped off his clothes, entered the water, and swam across to seize it.

As the royal household was urgently seeking sandalwood, he immediately loaded it onto a carriage and sent it to the palace. He received one million pieces of gold; the treasures he obtained were beyond measure.
Together with his brothers, he spoke in verse, saying:
"Diligence is foremost; With valor one can enter the sea And procure all manner of precious treasures To provide for one's family and kinsmen."
"Relying on me, he crossed the river waters, obtained exquisite sandalwood, and brought back a certain amount of gold; he consumed it himself and gave it to others.
This was the fifth merit. He then proceeded to a great kingdom.
At that time, the weather was hot; he lay beneath a tree, and when the sun had passed its zenith, the shadows of the other trees shifted, yet the shadow where this man lay remained unmoving.
His majestic spirit was towering and sublime; he was upright and beautiful, like the sun and the moon.
When that king passed away, there was no crown prince to succeed him. The people deliberated, saying, "We must seek out a worthy man to serve as our sovereign!
They dispatched messengers in all directions to search throughout the land for one fit to be enthroned.
The messenger went on his inspection and saw this one man beneath a tree, a rarity in the world, lying there with the shade of the tree remaining unmoving. He thought to himself:
"This is no ordinary person; he should be the ruler of the land!"
He immediately went to inform the great ministers of the kingdom in detail of the beginning and end of the matter.

Thereupon, the ministers at once prepared their dignified attire, leading the way with mounted attendants; they donned their seals of office, crowns, and turbans, and set out in carriages and formal dress to go and welcome him.
Having completed his bath, the application of fragrant unguents, and the donning of his robes and headgear, he prostrated himself in audience and declared himself a subject.
Ascending the carriage, he entered the palace and stood facing south to issue his edict; thereupon the realm attained great peace, and wind and rain came at their proper seasons.
He immediately issued a command to those outside:
"There are four men to be summoned:
first, one of wisdom; second, one of skillful artistry; third, one of handsome appearance; and fourth, one of diligent effort. Bring them to the inner chamber."
They all assembled at once and were ordered to remain in attendance.
Then, King Puṇyavanta spoke in verse:
“Those who possess merit and virtue Shall become Śakra, Lord of the Devas.”
Even universal monarchs and Brahma kings, Possessing wisdom and skill, Being handsome and diligent,
All enter the gateway of merit And stand in attendance as servants.
"Then King Puṇyavanta appointed his brothers to high positions, each ensuring they found their proper place.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The one who was wise at that time was none other than Śāriputra."
The one skilled in arts was Aniruddha;
the one of handsome appearance was Ānanda;
and the one diligent in practice was Śūḍpa.
The King Puṇyavanta was none other than myself.
At that time, each of them praised their own particular excellence, considering themselves the foremost; they are just as they are today.
In the past, at that time, everyone in the world was not like me, and each lamented for themselves.
Now that I have attained the Way of the Buddha and am the Honored One of the Three Realms, they all return to me as my disciples; relying upon the Buddha, they obtain deliverance.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all were filled with joy.
**The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Malevolent Fox and the Crows, Number Twenty-Five** Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"That Devadatta is wicked and dangerous; those who indiscriminately praise him do not grasp the truth.
The bhikṣu Kokālika praised Devadatta, and Devadatta likewise praised the bhikṣu Kokālika.
Those two men were pointlessly and unreasonably praising one another.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One:
"Indeed, O Great Sage!"

Observe the bhikṣu Kokālika: though he relied upon the authentic scriptures and followed the teachings of the Dharma and Vinaya, having left the household life out of faith to become a śramaṇa, he nonetheless slandered Devadatta, taking what is wrong for what is right and failing to grasp the true meaning.
Furthermore, that Devadatta praised the bhikṣu Kokālika, taking what is wrong to be right and what is right to be wrong.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“These foolish and deluded ones do not merely praise one another perversely, taking the wrong as right and the right as wrong, in this present life; it was the same in previous lives.”
In the distant past, long ago, a eunuch passed away and his kinsmen immediately took him and cast him among the stumps of *chū* trees.
At that time, foxes, crows, and birds came to eat his flesh, and they all sighed and lamented together.
Among the trees, a crow spoke a verse to the fox:
“Your body is like that of a lion; Your head is like that of a seer;
Your fat is like that of the king of deer; How excellent, like a beautiful flower!”
Then, from within the tree, the *gūḍha-śṛgāla* (the hidden fox) praised him with a verse, saying:
“Who is this honored one upon the tree? His wisdom is foremost and supreme;
His brilliance illuminates the ten directions, Like a mass of purple-golden (*cāmīkara*) gold.”
Then the crow replied with a verse, saying:
"You are indeed a great lion; I have come because I wish to see you.
Your fat is like that of a deer king; Excellent! You have gained a beneficial purpose."
The *gū-fox* replied with a verse, saying:
"Through sincerity, trust, and true mutual understanding, we both praise each other’s utmost honesty.
Were one to gather together refined purple-gold (*cāmīkara*), this is what you ask me to consume."
At that time, not far from there, there was a great seer dwelling in seclusion, practicing the path with pure cultivation.
Hearing the fox and the crow alternately praising one another, he thought to himself:
"These types of beings are falsely extolling each other; all they say is empty, and not a single word is truthful."
He asked in verse:
"I have long observed your activities; having come to this, you both engage in double-tongued speech.
You hide yourselves within the trees, and together you feast upon human flesh."
Then the crow, filled with resentment, replied to the seer in verse:
"The lion and the peacock Both eat the flesh of birds;
Yet they shave their heads bald, Seeking their livelihood in succession."
The seer replied with a verse:
“The *cūta* tree is foul-smelling to the extreme, Detested by all birds, yet relied upon by many deer; It is like the discarded corpse of a eunuch.”
"You base and lowly creatures, all gathered here together to feed upon the body of a eunuch, yet you call yourselves superior men.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know: the vixen at that time was Devadatta;
the crow was Kokālika; and the seer was none other than the Bodhisattva."
At that time, they all praised one another, taking what was wrong to be right and what was right to be wrong;
it is the same even now. **The Sūtra on the Illness of a Bhikṣu Spoken by the Buddha, Number Twenty-Six** Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who was gravely ill and alone; he had no companions and no one to look after him, nor did he have medicine, clothing, or food. Unable to rise or move about, impurities flowed from him naturally.
Lying upon it, he looked in the four directions; seeing no one to come to his rescue, he sighed to himself:
"Today my body has neither savior nor protector!"
At that time, Ānanda saw this and went to inform the Buddha:
"Indeed, Great Sage!
Today my body has attained what I have never before experienced."
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great kindness and great compassion; he should mindfully bring relief to bhikṣus who suffer.
In the past, during incalculable kalpas, I rescued this bhikṣu from the affliction of illness, and I do so in this present life as well.
