Please extend your great compassion to rescue us from this peril and deliver us from this hardship; now is the time for that.
A Great Sage is difficult to encounter; he appears only once in hundreds of millions of ages for the sake of sentient beings."
“Please bestow your great compassion and deliver me by looking upon me but once.
The Buddha said, “Excellent!”
"How deeply pitiable! That the deluded mind should encounter such calamity.
Ānanda, along with the devas, nāgas, spirits, and humans, was all struck with astonishment, greatly wondering at the reason for this.
The class of animals has taken refuge in the World-Honored One.
Ānanda knelt long and asked the Holy Honored One:
"Why did these oxen, upon seeing the Buddha, take refuge in him?"
“What is the beginning and the end of this? The Buddha said:

“In the distant past, long ago, there was a Wheel-Turning King who ruled over the four quarters of the world. He possessed a thousand sons and the seven treasures; he governed by the True Dharma and did not oppress the myriad people. The world was at peace, the populace was tranquil, and the five grains were abundant.”
Furthermore, there are four virtues:
he regards the people as his own children, and the people revere him as a father;
among śramaṇas, brahmins, elders, and commoners, there are none who do not treat him with filial affection.
His body has never been ill and he enjoys eternal peace;
his virtue is proclaimed throughout the four quarters and reaches to the ten directions.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, having traveled to observe the four regions, desired to return to his palace.
At that time, he saw a kinsman from a former life who had been seized by creditors and bound to a tree, unable to move.
The Wheel-Turning King, accompanied by his retinue of the seven treasures, halted and did not proceed, wondering at the cause of this.
"From afar, I see an old friend of mine who has been detained by others; he owes fifty taels of gold and is being prevented from leaving.
The Holy King replied to him:
"Release him and let him go; I shall give you double that amount, one hundred taels of gold."
The man replied, "I have further incurred a debt of one hundred taels of gold for someone else, which I must repay; I cannot let it go.
The Holy King then issued an edict to his ministers and subordinates:
"Go to the palace and give him one hundred taels of gold.
The subordinate official replied, "Yes!"
He immediately paid off his creditors and was able to return home.
However, that man went repeatedly to the gate of the royal palace, seeking gold but failing to obtain it.
While the creditor sought him, he avoided him so that the creditor did not know his whereabouts.

Thus, wandering through birth and death for countless kalpas, he has not repaid his debts; until this present life, he has fallen among cattle. For the thousands of taels of gold he owes and for which he was sold, he has now come to take refuge in the Buddha, drawn by the牵引 (karmic attraction) of past conditions.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“At that time, the wheel-turning king was none other than myself;
the creditor was this very ox.”
The Buddha was once a holy king who guaranteed a debt for him, yet ultimately did not repay it; therefore, he has come to the Buddha to seek the recovery of his debt and deliverance.
The Buddha told the owner of the oxen:
"I shall act as a mendicant on your behalf to repay you twofold."
The owner of the ox was unwilling to comply and wished to have his ox back.
The Buddha spoke to him again:
"I shall weigh the ox's body against a certain number of *jin* of gold."
Therefore, he was unwilling!
At that time, Śakra and Brahmā descended together and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
"Buddha, do not go on almsround!"
"Whatever gold you desire to obtain—ten thousand, a hundred million, or a billion taels—we shall provide it for you.
They spread out two ox-hides, and Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings piled up gold and jewels until the two ox-hides were completely filled; only then did they each withdraw.

Leading the ox into the Jeta Grove, he entered through its middle gate and observed the body of the Buddha and the forms of the holy assembly. The virtues of the various bodhisattvas were sublime and immeasurable; they were radiant and majestic, like the moon among the stars, their divine power illuminating afar beyond all calculation.

While reflecting during that time, he called to mind the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; when his life ended after seven days, he was suddenly reborn in the heavens. Immediately recollecting and recognizing his own past lives and the virtues of the World-Honored One, he returned to the human realm, scattered flowers as an offering to the Buddha to repay his benevolence, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.

The Buddha preached the sutra for them, whereupon they immediately conceived the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment and instantly attained the stage of non-retrogression through the patience of non-arising; thereafter, they returned to the heavens.
40. The Sūtra on the Brahmin Prabhāsa Spoken by the Buddha. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and an incalculable number of bodhisattvas.

At that time, incalculable thousands of people all gathered at the place where the Buddha was; they all shaved their hair and beards and became śramaṇas. Each, with a retinue of five hundred followers, cultivated the Way and its virtue, practicing with diligence and without slackening. They attained supernormal powers, severed the roots of birth and death, universally realized the fruits of the Path, and traveled throughout the ten directions to deliver sentient beings.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:

"What practices did these members of the assembly perform in their past lives, and what virtues did they originally cultivate, such that they have attained this renown and the wisdom of supernormal powers, becoming foremost among them?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha."
There was a king named Candra, whose capital city was called Candramatī.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Prabhāsa, who was profoundly learned in the various scriptures and widely proclaimed the Dharma texts, such that there was no meaning he did not comprehend;
he had a retinue of five hundred followers who attended upon him to receive his teachings.

He went repeatedly to visit the Tathāgata Vipaśyin to listen to and receive the sūtras; he exhorted and transformed the masses, enlightening those who were ignorant and deluded, and encouraged them toward the correct and true path, practicing as a śramaṇa with the cultivation of virtue as his vocation.
At that time, five hundred attendants from that country, along with five hundred great ministers and officials, also became śramaṇas.

There was a great elder who converted the multitude, causing them all to likewise leave the household life and practice as śramaṇas, where they practiced with diligence and did not violate the prohibitions and precepts.
After their lives ended, they were reborn in the heavens.
When their lifespans in the heavens expired, they returned to birth in the human realm.

Thus, ascending and descending, ending and beginning again, for ninety-one kalpas within this Buddha-world, they all became śramaṇas; they all assembled at the Buddha’s dwelling, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew to sit to one side.

Devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all came without exception to where the Buddha was; they prostrated at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Buddha smiled.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"For what cause and condition do you smile?"
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, never rejoices in vain; he speaks only according to the underlying intent.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see these multitudes of humans, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits who have gathered here?"
He replied, “I have seen them.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin, there was a great kingdom named Cāndramatī, and its king was named Candra; they all upheld the Great Dharma and took refuge in the Triple Gem."

At that time, there was a brahmin named Guanghua (Prabhāsa), who possessed the three types of supernormal knowledge and had extensively mastered the various scriptures; there was no meaning he did not comprehend. Seeing the Buddha Vipaśyin transforming beings throughout the ten directions, and observing that from the heavens above to the earth below there were none whom he did not inspire with faith, he led a multitude of five hundred followers to the Buddha’s abode to become śramaṇas, and they all received the sūtras and the precepts.
At that time, the king of that country abandoned his kingdom and renounced his royalty, becoming a śramaṇa along with a retinue of five hundred.

There was also a great elder who likewise transformed his followers—a group of five hundred—to practice as śramaṇas; they all received the transformation of the Way, advanced to attain supernatural powers, and upheld the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. For ninety-one kalpas, they did not return to the evil realms, but were born among gods and humans; now having obtained human bodies, they have all come to this assembly. They too have universally left the household life to become śramaṇas, receiving the sūtras and precepts, and have all attained realization of the Way.
If you wish to know whether the brahmin who practiced at that time was anyone else, do not hold such a view; it was none other than my own self.

The king, the people, and the assembly of great elders were all fellow students of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, Vipaśyin, at that same time. What they sowed there, they have reaped here; their merit has not been in vain, and each has attained it for themselves.

When the Buddha spoke these words, countless people all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; at that moment, they were established in the stage of non-retrogression, and those who were in their final birth before Buddhahood were likewise beyond calculation, as were those who attained the state of Arhat.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, all were filled with joy.
**Sūtra 41: The Discourse on the Parable of Regret** Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a householder who grew weary of the suffering and afflictions of the world and the impermanence of all things. He perceived that all the wealth and possessions belonging to the body are like illusions; dwelling between heaven and earth is like being a passing guest, with nothing at all to crave.

Realizing only the true and correct Way can endure forever, he consequently left the household life to become a śramaṇa. He practiced with diligent and tireless effort, yet when his original aspiration remained unfulfilled, he entered the mountains.

Practicing in the mountains, he did not cease his efforts day or night; he did not spare his own body or life, practicing generosity, observing the precepts, enduring with patience, exerting himself with diligence, and maintaining single-minded wisdom. Yet, though his will remained unshakable, he failed to attain realization of the Way, and his mind began to waver and regret, wishing to return to the life of a layman:
"I have studied the Way for many years, laboring without rest, yet my mind remains dark and obscured, and I know not where it is headed."

"Originally, while among men, I frequently received instruction and discussion; my words flowed abundantly. Now, being here in the mountains, I have gained nothing further. Since there is no benefit in advancing or retreating, and I do not know where to turn, it would be better to cast off these robes and return to my former occupation."

Hesitating and undecided, the mountain spirits and tree deities beheld him; they grieved that his labor, which was on the verge of accomplishment, would instead lead him back home with his mind fixed upon impurities. Their resentment on his behalf was beyond compare.
Thereupon, she transformed herself into the body of a bhikṣuṇī. She intentionally manifested a distracted mind to inspire the aspiration for the Way and to strengthen her resolve.

This bhikṣuṇī was adorned with precious jewels, and her complexion was radiant and glorious, unlike anything in the world. Furthermore, she appeared as a woman of upright countenance and supreme beauty; her form was so brilliant and resplendent that none among the multitude could equal her.
They spoke to one another, saying:
"O Bhikṣuṇī, for what reason do you wear these precious necklaces?
Your lips and mouth are exquisitely beautiful, like red pearls."
The bhikṣuṇī said: "Jewels are like illusory transformations; lips are like painted colors; beauty is like a coating of oil—what is there to crave?

Your body now, though its form is as beautiful as a spring flower, is like a fruit that has fallen and will not remain upon the tree for long. It is a mere conglomeration and dispersion of the four great elements, possessing no true master."
Mind alone is the foundation; within the three realms, one comes and goes entirely alone with no one following. Misfortune and fortune pursue the person like a shadow follows a form.

All three realms are empty, and there is nothing upon which to rely; shrouded by transgressions, the five aggregates and six hindrances close the mind and block the intellect, preventing the realization of samādhi.

Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu immediately attained awakening and realized that it was exactly as stated: he discerned that the four great elements arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; that attachment to the body leads to self-harm; and that when analyzed, they are fundamentally empty, like a temporary lodging. Observing the people of the ten directions, he found no distinction between kin and stranger. Thus his mind became clear and his intellect was liberated; all outflows were exhausted, birth and death were severed, and there was no longer any arising of conditioned existence. His coming and going became free, and he remained unstained by defilement. Only then did he thoroughly understand that because the mountains and trees have a basis, their transformation is like the clearing away of floating clouds.
The tree spirit knelt and prostrated, declaring:

"I have labored in my circuit through the three realms, shrouded by the five aggregates and entangled by the twelve links. Having suddenly begun this causal succession, I pray only that you take pity on me and deliver me from this obscuration."

He immediately preached the sutra for them, causing their minds to open and be liberated. They received and upheld the five precepts, practiced the ten wholesome deeds, and blocked off the three evil realms. Their aspiration for the Way gradually advanced until they reached the ultimate, entering the Buddha’s true and correct path.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Understand its beginning and end; hold fast with resolve, lest you later regret it.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was none who did not rejoice.

**Sūtra on the Parable of the Horse, Spoken by the Buddha, Number Forty-Two** In the past, there was an elder who kept a fine horse. When he first obtained it, its disposition was to bolt and charge recklessly, such that it could not be controlled or tamed.

Just as he was about to be mounted, he raised his two front legs, leaped up, and bolted away; he ran crosswise in all directions, refusing to follow the path, entering ditches and channels, and charging against trees and walls.
The master, the elder, harbored intense resentment; upon returning home, he whipped and beat him with cruel severity, withholding water and grass, leaving him utterly destitute.
Afflicted by hunger and mental distress, he reproached himself; with no plan in mind, he did not know what to offer.
Then a voice issued from the air, addressing him:
"If you obey your master, there will be no calamity."

At that time, the horse’s mind was liberated. The next day, when the elder again mounted it for trial and placed the saddle and bridle upon it, the horse immediately accepted them and no longer reared or kicked.

When mounted on its saddle, it does not display any restlessness; whether led east, west, south, or north, it follows along without opposition. One provides it with grain and drink, regulating the amounts according to the season to ensure it remains full, robust, and possesses great strength.
Later, when the horse was about to go out riding, it became increasingly docile and grew more accomplished day by day.
Subsequently, two sons were born; when they reached the age of several years, the elder son would ride upon it.

Later, the horse became disobedient, leaping and galloping wildly until it snapped its reins and broke its harness. Although he struck it with whips and canes, it did not reform its behavior, so he returned home and starved it.
He then reflected upon his own misfortune: "I eat stinking grass and drink from turbid springs; having created this myself, I must receive its consequences—what more is there to resent?
Walking at night, he saw his mother, knelt down, and asked her:
"Now, my mistress alone treats me with such hatred and cruelty; I cannot find water or grass, and the lashes of her whip are most severe."

The mother alone stood on high, not mindful of her kin; she moved about with joy, her single body filled with delight. Looking far out from her lofty vantage, she was like a great swan, unconcerned that her children and grandchildren would alone encounter such cruelty.
His mother replied:
"This is your own fault; why should you resent or blame anyone?
Once the elder has given you the bridle and the saddle, you must simply accept the ride and follow him obediently wherever he goes, east or west, and then you will surely be loved!"
"This matter is extremely simple, yet you have acted contrary to it; therefore, you have incurred this calamity!
Having heard his mother’s instruction, the son followed it immediately the next day.
The elder tested him, and he remained calm and compliant; when the elder mounted him and directed his body, he would move as soon as told to go and stop as soon as told to stay.
The elder was greatly pleased, and the horse immediately became well-trained and docile; it received food and drink at the proper times, no different from its mother.

To take this as a metaphor: the elder represents the Buddha, and the horse represents the student. Because the student does not accept the Buddha's teachings, letting their mind run wild and acting according to their own whims, they do not follow the transformation of the Path; therefore, the Dharma is preached for them to make them understand what to abandon and what to pursue.

To those who leap about and run wild, beyond restraint, he applies the cane and staff; for them, he expounds the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions so they may be reborn among devas and humans. To those who have committed offenses, he shows the sufferings and hardships of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, as well as the afflictions of the three realms, wherein beings transmigrate and revolve without a single place of peace.

If they do not commit evil, one then instructs them in the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions; through the four immeasurables, the six perfections, and the practice of supernatural powers, they gather in the assemblies of the Buddhas of the ten directions, eliminate the three poisons, and remove all hindrances and obscurations.

The son followed his mother and knelt for a long time, asking: "Previously, I heard of the rules of conduct practiced by my teacher; my teacher said that whether the practices were profound or shallow, they all possessed meaning.

Thus, the five precepts and ten wholesome acts are taught as causes for becoming a celestial or human being. Furthermore, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the six perfections (pāramitās); and the four immeasurables and four debts of gratitude—these do not abide in birth-and-death, nor do they dwell in extinction (nirvāṇa). Rather, they lead one into the True and Right, for those of courageous resolve who dwell in the vehicle of supernormal powers, traverse the three realms, and deliver all beings."

43. The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Manifestations of the Bhikṣuṇīs. The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Manifestations of the Bhikṣuṇīs, Number Forty-Three. In the past, there was a city named Śrāvastī, and the name of that city was Kauśāmbī.

In the kingdom there was a multitude of dissolute and licentious people who were exclusively devoted to cruelty and evil; they did not follow the proper path, and the entire nation suffered from them, regarding them as a bitter affliction. These companions pursued one another and together committed acts of rebellion and malice; though the authorities sought to apprehend them, they fled and could not be caught.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs in the kingdom were traveling together, dwelling under trees with single-minded devotion, contemplating the Right Path without abandoning their resolve.
Among these bhikṣuṇīs, the foremost in wisdom was named Kṣema;
the foremost in supernormal powers was named Padmāvatī. Each possessed virtuous conduct, and their majestic spiritual power was sublime.

At that time, as the weather was somewhat warm, they all went to wash themselves and approached the side of a flowing stream. From afar, the wicked crowd saw them and immediately conceived evil thoughts; their lustful intentions surged, and they desired to violate them.

While waiting for the bhikṣuṇī, who had just removed her robes and entered the water to bathe, he immediately went forward, snatched away her clothes, and took them to a distant place, intending to violate her.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī, seeing that he had conceived such rebellious thoughts, felt a deep sense of sorrow in her heart; pitying him for his folly, she then plucked out both her eyes, placed them in his palms, and showed them to the various rebels.
"You love me," he said, "but you love only my facial features; now that I am blind, what is there left to find attractive?
He then displayed his intestines, stomach, the five viscera, hands, and feet, each separated from one another, casting them aside to one side, and addressed the onlookers:
"Where is that which you call 'beautiful'?"

Upon seeing this, Niexiong was suddenly struck with terror; he realized that the world is impermanent, that the three realms are like a temporary lodging, and that his own body is subject to transformation, consisting of impure bones and blood, nothing of which is worth craving.
They immediately returned their robes and prostrated themselves to repent, saying:
"What we have done is improper and contrary to righteousness; we pray that you will absolve us of this calamity.
They knelt long with palms joined and each received the five precepts.
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated himself upon the ground and reproached himself for his transgressions:

“Blind and ignorant, I have been lost in delusion for a long time; I committed evils without ceasing, unaware that I would suffer calamity and peril life after life. Now, having received the grace of the Great Sage’s salvation, I am moved by the Bhikṣuṇī’s majestic virtue which has restored my sight; my sins are lightened, and I draw closer to the state of non-action.”
The Buddha said: "Excellent!
You have already left the evil realms behind and shall soon achieve fulfillment. Just as the branches of a tree bear flowers and the fruits grow lush, so too shall your practice follow from this."
The people were delighted and requested to become śramaṇas.
The Buddha immediately granted them permission, saying:
"Taking the rectification of the mind as the foundation."

He immediately left the household life, guarded his sense faculties, and forever eliminated all calamities; the five hindrances ceased to exist, the three poisons were extinguished, and he became a son of the Buddha. Having severed birth and death, he spontaneously attained supernormal powers, and only then did he discern the great kindness of the Buddha.

44. The Sūtra on Solitude Spoken by the Buddha. The Sūtra on Solitude Spoken by the Buddha, Number Forty-Four. In the past, there was a man who had been orphaned and suffering since childhood, living all alone.

He cultivated extensive fields, increasing his number of plow-oxen, and harvested the five grains, milk, curd, and clarified butter (ghṛta). His various fruits and vegetables were beyond measure, providing for all who ate them from near and far; he constantly assisted those in poverty as they came and went, and his fame and virtue spread throughout the ten directions.

At that time, he spoke various parables to cause them to understand his meaning: "One cannot succeed alone; one must have companions. When many people all come together and dwell together, their households will gradually increase by the side of that person, and cities and towns will eventually be established."
He took a wife and fathered many sons. As his father grew old, he instructed his sons:
"You must act accordingly: guard your body, speech, and mind, and practice generosity and virtue."
The sons each acted in opposition and did not follow his instructions.
"Our father is now already old; why does he not remain in tranquility?
He teaches falsely; who would accept it?"
The father, distressed by his sons, thought to himself:

"I originally had but one body, with which I bestowed abundant gifts far and wide, reaching even down to those who were destitute. Now that I have these sons, they disturb my mind and body; since they do not follow my instructions, it would be better for me to have no sons at all."
The Buddha said:
“A person originally establishes a spirit; when the body is clear and pure, it can be of benefit.

Yet, while they uphold right practice and exert themselves in contemplation, they do not understand that all is fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*). Seeing themselves as having a body, they consequently give rise to the delusions of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the six decays (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Thus, they are instead bewildered by these very things and fail to reach the state of true reality.”

Later, he realized that all things in the three realms are empty, the five aggregates are entirely eliminated, and the three poisons naturally extinguish themselves, leading even to the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was no one who did not rejoice.
The Birth Sūtra, Scroll Four;

45. The Discourse on the Brahmin Spoken by the Buddha.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms; proceeding from house to house in search of food, he eventually arrived at the residence of a brahmin.
At that time, the brahmin saw from afar the World-Honored One— his majestic spiritual power towering and sublime,
his faculties serene and stilled, his mind profoundly tranquil, having subdued all the senses and being free from further decline or influx— like the sun rising over a mountain ridge,
like the full moon shining uniquely bright among the multitude of stars, like the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, situated in its place.
Like Śakra in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, like the Brahmā King among the Brahmās, like a great mass of snow upon a high mountain appearing from afar in the four directions,
like a tree in full bloom, his mind serene and tranquil; like the clarity of water,
his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks and his form was suffused with the eighty minor characteristics, radiant with majestic spiritual power.

His radiance was beyond measure; beholding him was like seeing the sun. He immediately rose from his seat and, together with his retinue, went forward to welcome him, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and invited him to sit upon a separate couch.
The Buddha then took his seat.
At that time, the brahmin and his wife, their hearts filled with exultation, personally served and presented various kinds of food and fragrant, pure delicacies in boundless abundance as an offering.
When the meal was finished, they set aside their bowls, washed their hands, and took up low stools to listen to the Buddha preach the sutras.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Way of the sutras for the brahmin, his wife, children, and servants, opening their minds and discerning the meanings for them. He expounded and analyzed the Dharma of all Buddhas according to its original source: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom. Like administering medicine according to the ailment, he taught the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Thereupon, their minds were liberated.

At that time, the brahmin’s wife, children, servants, and subordinates attained the Four Noble Truths while still on their seats; in brief, they obtained the divine eye, took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and received the five precepts.
Thereupon, the brahmin rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The Great Sage has bestowed vast grace, manifesting immediate benefit and profit. What I have attained today—being delivered from all afflictions—is entirely due to the salvation provided by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. It is like a great cloud that encompasses the void and rains universally upon the world, providing abundant moisture.”
"The World-Honored One is thus; with constant, great compassion and boundless kindness, he extensively expounds the Great Dharma.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you wish to hear what the brahmin has now proclaimed and what he says with his own mouth?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
I have seen it; I have heard it.”
The Buddha said:
"Now this brahmin and his retinue have all attained great benefit, being thus fully endowed with it;
in another age, I shall cause this brahmin to attain it extensively and universally."

In the distant past, long ago, there was in the city of Vārāṇasī a venerable one named Rakṣita, who was of the brahmin caste. He was wise and intelligent, possessed a thorough understanding of principles and meanings, and his responses were eloquent; his speech was graceful and pleasing, such that he was honored by the king and always acted in accordance with the king’s wishes.
That country abounded in wine, grape juices, and various implements for food and drink; both the king and the people enjoyed themselves in feasting and pleasure.
At that time, the brahmin performed extraordinary arts and provided much entertainment, causing the king to be filled with joy and wonder.
The King was greatly delighted and bestowed many gifts upon him,
saying, "Have whatever you desire!
The brahmin addressed the King:
"I shall return home and ask my wife what it is she desires to seek.
The King consented to this.
The Brahmin then returned home and asked his wife:
"I have performed extraordinary arts to cause the King to rejoice and grant my wish. What do you seek?
Tell me with sincerity, and I shall procure it for you."
The wife asked the brahmin,
"What is your wish? Her husband replied:
"I wish for an entire district," his wife replied.
"What use is seeking a district? I wish to obtain a hundred kinds of necklaces and ornaments, such as armlets and anklets; various garments; slaves; and milk, curd, clarified butter, and food."
At that time, the brahmin again asked his son, "What do you seek? His son replied:
"My wish is that I do not have to travel on foot, but may instead ride in a carriage or on horseback while traveling together with the Prince and his ministers.
At that time, the Brahmin again asked his daughter,
"What is your aspiration?"

The girl replied, "What I seek is to obtain jewels to adorn my body and exquisite garments to wear, so that I may be uniquely beautiful in the midst of a thousand women; what need have I for any other extraordinary wish?"
At that time, the brahmin again asked the male and female slaves,
"What do you seek to aspire to?

"How unprecedented! A single person has appeared in the world, titled Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he has destroyed all the various heterodox teachers, so that they have suddenly fallen into darkness and no longer possess any radiance."

Before the appearance of a Buddha, those who offered exquisite offerings—of clothing, food and drink, and bedding—and served him with reverence, taking refuge in him, found that such words of instruction were not practiced once a Buddha appeared in the world.
With his divine ear, the Buddha heard from afar what the bhikṣus were discussing together; he went to where they were and asked the bhikṣus, "What were you discussing just now?"
The bhikṣus fully reported, saying:

"When we gathered together, the Perfectly Enlightened One had just arisen in the world; all those of other heterodox paths immediately vanished and were no longer seen, suddenly falling into darkness without any further radiance."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Before I appeared in the world, the teachings of outsiders flourished; it was as if there were no sun or moon, and only the light of torches served as illumination.
Once the sun and moon had arisen, the torches possessed no light."

Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, the heterodox teachers have all vanished, their majestic splendor no longer remaining; only the Buddha’s wisdom and brilliance shine everywhere, illuminating all things.
It is not only in this present life that he possesses such extraordinary conduct; it was likewise so in previous lives, for there has never been a dharma like his.
In the distant past, long ago, there was a great kingdom located in the borderlands of the north, known as Jihuan (Jiànhuàn).
The people of Jihuan took crows with them and traveled to the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.
In that land and its borders, there were no such crows, nor were there any other kinds of extraordinary or marvelous birds.

When the people of that country saw the crow being brought, they leaped for joy, unable to contain themselves; they made offerings and served it with food, drink, fruits, and melons, day after day and month after month.
He then sent out word of this.
Crows from distant lands, upon learning of it, all came to assemble in numbers beyond counting; the entire nation collectively made offerings and served him with immeasurable reverence.

At another time, there was a merchant who arrived from another country bringing three peacocks. When the people saw them, they found them to be exquisitely beautiful and extraordinary; their plumage was unique, and their gait was harmonious and elegant—unprecedented in their experience.
The multitude beheld this together and heard his voice; their hearts leaped with joy, a thousand million times greater than before, and they all abandoned the crow, no longer serving it.

The crows lost their majestic luster and suddenly became colorless; like the rising sun that causes candlelight to vanish, they no longer had any thought remaining among the crows. They came to love and revere the peacock entirely, gazing upon it without weariness.

All the implements previously used for honoring and nourishing the crows were now used to make offerings to the form of the peacock; they paid homage with deep respect and took refuge in him, until all the crows vanished, their whereabouts unknown.
At that time, there was a deva who uttered this verse in praise:
"When the light of the sun has not yet appeared, The lamp alone provides illumination;
The crows, by their very nature, perceive their tasks: Drinking water and eating fruits."
Because his voice was perfect, when the sun rose he would rest among the trees;
there, all the crows would come to pay him homage, yet now that is forever gone.
One should contemplate this excellence: in his service, there were no distinctions of high or low.
“If the Honored One had not appeared at his own will, the lowly would have no one to revere.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, inspired by the World-Honored One’s teaching, felt a surge of joy and praised him in verse:
“If the Buddha had not arisen, if the Guide had not appeared in the world...”
All the outside śramaṇas and brahmins were universally provided with offerings and service;
now that the Buddha possesses the perfect voice and expounds the Dharma with clarity,
those various classes of heterodox practitioners have forever lost all their offerings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who the peacock was at that time, it was I myself;
the crows were the various non-Buddhist heterodox teachers."
"The Deva" was Ānanda.

Although he preached the Dharma while in the world, he had not yet eliminated the three poisons or birth, old age, sickness, and death; he could not ultimately remove the defilements of worldly toil and purely cultivate the Brahma-faring.

Now the Tathāgata has appeared in the world—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He now preaches the Dharma, complete and ultimate; he has purely cultivated the Brahma-faring, leaving behind all dust and defilement; he has eliminated lust, anger, and delusion, as well as birth, old age, sickness, and death; he walks alone through the triple world without fear, subduing all heterodox groups and external teachers so that none do not submit, and all receive his deliverance.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, all were filled with joy.
**The Sūtra on the Seer Bālakalpa Spoken by the Buddha, Number Fifty-Two** Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the elder Jinjinshou went to where Śāriputra was and recited the sūtras and the Dharma.

Upon returning to his home, he grew weary of his dwelling and shaved off his beard and hair to become a śramaṇa. Although he had not yet attained arhatship, everything required for his practice was already fully prepared.
Then the bhikṣus went to see the World-Honored One and said:
"Now we have examined our lives to their end; with heads bowed, we come before you in person to hear the Dharma and Vinaya, and immediately we shall go forth to become śramaṇas."

Possessing extensive learning and great wisdom, he expounded various dharmas; his discourse was elegant and refined, his demeanor composed and free from turbulence. Having aroused the mind of meditative reflection, he therefore returned home once more.
“World-Honored One!

It is thus: for those who have not yet attained arhatship as appropriate to their capacity, there is the rootless and unattached Dharma; because they have not yet achieved it, they behold the cycle of birth and death and its revolving turns, failing to attain liberation. This is as taught by the Buddha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—and is the peace and security he has realized.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What is there to marvel at?

When I attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and became the Most Perfectly Awakened One, although Śāriputra was already being taught and delivered from the four afflictions by me with my own hands, it is truly extraordinary that in another age, while still in the body of an ordinary person, I extensively expounded the sūtras and dharmas to deliver all those undergoing toil and suffering."
In the distant past, long ago, there was a seer named Bala who had attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

At that time, he was honored and served by the king with immeasurable love and respect; possessing the power of spiritual travel, he would fly back and forth between the royal palace and his own abode.
At that time, the king provided for the seer with all manner of offerings and comfort; he sat beside him every day in this manner.

The king served the seer, spreading his hair upon the ground for him to walk upon, and personally portioned out a hundred kinds of food and drink. He did so for many years, providing for him without limit.

At that time, the king had some minor business to attend to. He had a daughter who was upright and beautiful, rare in the world; the king held her in high esteem and cherished her beyond measure, yet she had not yet stepped out of the palace gates.
The king said to his daughter:
"Do you see me? I serve the rishi with such earnest devotion that I dare not let my mind stray from him."
The woman replied, "Indeed, I have seen it.
The king said to her:
"Now I have business and must travel far; you shall provide for him, and you must serve him as I do, without failing in your attentions.
At that time, the rishi descended from the air and arrived within the royal palace. When the princess saw him coming, she received him with her hands and seated him upon a throne.

As soon as he supported it with his hand, he felt its body was soft and supple; immediately, a desire arose within him. As that lustful mind emerged, his craving intensified, and he instantly lost his supernormal power of the feet, so that he could no longer fly.
He practiced walking meditation with focused reflection, wishing to regain his supernormal powers, yet he was unable to achieve them.

At that time, the seer beheld the king’s daughter, and a mind of lust arose within him; being unable to fulfill his desire, he departed from the palace on foot. As he did so, his cries rang out so loudly that there was no one who did not hear and know of it.
At that time, an incalculable number of people all gathered together.

When the King had finished his duties and returned to his palace, he heard that the seer had lost his state of desirelessness and fallen into the midst of affection; having lost his supernormal power, he was no longer able to fly.
At that time, the king went to the hermitage at night; moving alone and in secret, he went to see the seer, prostrated at his feet, and spoke in verse:
"I have heard that the great brahmacārin is prone to sudden outbursts of greed and desire;
by what teaching does he act thus?"
"For what reason do you practice sensual desire?
Then the seer Bālaka replied to the king in verse:
"I am indeed so, O Great King, As has been heard by the noble ones."
"Having already fallen onto a wrong path, it is because the King has distanced himself from me.
The King asked in verse:
"I do not know where your wisdom lies, nor what you contemplate as good or evil."
"Even if one were to give rise to a mind of desire,
one could not overcome fundamental purity.
Then, the seer Bālakrīḍa replied to the king in verse:
“Sensual desire ruins one’s welfare; the lustful mind burns with stifling intensity.
Having heard the King’s words today, I shall immediately renounce sensual desire.”
At that time, the king instructed the rishi.
The rishi felt ashamed and reproached himself with all his heart; through diligent effort throughout the night, he soon regained his supernatural powers.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The seer Vikalpa of that time was none other than Śāriputra;
the king was my own self."
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all were filled with joy.
**Sūtra on the Lay Disciple Ayīśāṃti and His Son, Spoken by the Buddha**, Number Fifty-Three. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

There was a lay devotee who had a son who was intelligent, wise, and eloquent. In whatever he undertook, there was nothing he did not master; he was able to establish himself and remained diligent, possessing exceptional clarity and discernment.
Furthermore, he understood the profits of household business and trade, thereby acquiring great wealth and treasures with which he supported his parents.
Protected by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and guarded by the devas, he was beloved and respected by countless people.

Displeasing his father’s will, he was neither loved nor cared for by him; his father constantly loathed the sight of him, drove him out of the house, and repeatedly beat him with sticks and canes. Unable to endure it any longer, he fled to another country.

Residing in a foreign land, he engaged in trade and commerce for a livelihood; through skillful means and careful calculation, he undertook various enterprises, never missing the proper seasons and not neglecting his business, thereby accumulating great wealth and treasures.
The lay devotee, hearing that [his son] had accumulated much wealth and treasure, sent messengers from afar to summon him to return home; however, the son was unwilling to return.
The lay devotee sent messengers again, instructing them: "If he does not come, send the wealth and goods instead."
Though he earnestly exhorted and instructed him, the father was utterly unwilling to let him go. His son replied:
"My father’s distress toward me is beyond measure; it has reached the point where I cannot even bring myself to send him away, nor can I bear to go there myself."
At that time, the lay devotee (upāsaka) spoke to the assembly of bhikṣus, confessing his thoughts:
"My son is ill, yet he does not comply with his parents.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:

"This lay devotee was not only at odds with his son in this life, but it was likewise so in previous lives. His merit and virtue were extraordinary; whatever deeds he performed, he never failed or erred, yet [his son] could not bear his heart."
"Monk, observe this: that son’s wisdom is extraordinary and his virtue immeasurable; one cannot satisfy his mind, nor can one wish to hear his voice, yet one desires to contemplate and attain it."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, long ago, there was a man named Ārāda Śāṇḍilya who was a teacher of monkeys. He taught the monkeys the rules of movement and various skills and acrobatics, which brought great delight to the masses of people."
By means of this craft, countless people all came to love and respect him; from far and near they all came to witness his skill, and through this grace, many obtained wealth and profit.
Āryaśāṇḍilya had previously kept a monkey that had acquired a great deal of goods; he would beat, strike, and trample it.
On another day, the man took the monkey into the city, bound it to a pillar, and subjected it to painful beatings, insults, and humiliation.

At that time, the monkey secretly slipped away in silence, rushed into the mountains, and dwelt in solitude. He drew near to the seer, relying on him for shelter; he gathered fruits and melons to provide for the seer, while also eating them himself.
When Āryaśāṇḍilya heard this, he went to that secluded mountain and sent a messenger to summon him back.
The monkey refused and replied from afar:

"I am still mindful of how you previously tormented me with poison; my sufferings were immeasurable. At that time, my father was falsely accused of no fault and subjected to poison; the insults he suffered were beyond description. It is for these reasons that I have fled and entered these mountains."
Ārṣabha went there himself and said to the monkey,
"Come back home. But the monkey remained silent and refused.
The seer replied,
"It may indeed be left as it is.
He answered the seer, saying:
"I shall leave it at that," [the king] replied.
The rishi reported, "It may not be forcibly brought; one should first offer some gentle exhortation, and only then lead him away."
"Even if one were to force oneself to go there,
it may still not be possible. The man replied,
"If you employ skillful means to bring him away and he is still unwilling to go, I shall devise a plan."
Immediately, he sang this verse in praise:
"You are a virtuous, gentle, and good son; Like a deer seeking shade, you have descended from the branch of the tree, And thus avoided death from hunger and thirst."
Then the monkey replied in verse:
"Harshness and lack of benevolence gave birth to me; I myself know my own disposition.
From what I have seen and heard, I am a gentle and virtuous monkey."
I have gone forth in all directions, yet I have had no intermediate thoughts;
even if false growths were to arise, they could never restrain my mind.
I now maintain this mindfulness continuously—O Ārya Śāṇakavāsin!
They led me into the city, bound me to a pillar, and inflicted upon me agonizing pain.
Even now I do not forget how they beat and struck me with bitter cruelty;
yet having attained self-mastery, I cannot submit to your oppression.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who was Āryaśāṇḍilyaputra at that time, he is this present lay devotee;
as for the lay devotee, he is the father of today."
"The seer was none other than myself.
Such was his full accomplishment; this I shall now explain in detail.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was no one who did not rejoice.
54. The Discourse on Husband and Wife Spoken by the Buddha. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

There was a lay follower whose wife was upright and beautiful, with a most excellent countenance and a majestic radiance that was peerless in its splendor. She was intelligent and wise, possessed eloquence in speech, brought much joy to others, and was revered by all.
At that time, her husband did not respect or honor her; he loathed her and took no pleasure in her, having no desire even to see her.
Instead, he came to respect and love an elderly servant woman who was neither diligent nor beautiful, taking her as his concubine and holding her in high esteem.
When his wife saw that her husband’s mind was alienated and discordant, and that his aspirations were set upon serving others, she said to him:
"If it is the case that your heart does not find joy in me, perhaps you would grant me leave to leave the household life for the Way and become a bhikṣuṇī."
After she had repeatedly entreated him in this manner, her husband finally consented.
She immediately left the household life to pursue the Way as a bhikṣuṇī; practicing the Path with diligence day and night, before long she realized arhatship.
However, at a later time, the woman whom that lay devotee (upāsaka) had venerated passed away.
Thereupon, the lay devotee went in search of her and found his former wife as a bhikṣuṇī; he called her to return to his home.
The bhikṣuṇī was unwilling to comply with him, saying:
"I have already left the household life and thus belong to another; furthermore, we have been reborn in different worlds, and our karmic retributions for sin and merit are not the same.
When the bhikṣuṇī heard this, she went to inform the World-Honored One, recounting the matter from beginning to end.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This lay devotee did not only in this present life disparage and insult this virtuous person; he had done so in previous lives as well.
Furthermore, this woman has been possessed of virtue and an extraordinary resolve in birth after birth, yet this man has constantly sought to corrupt and disrupt her."
"Now these bhikṣuṇīs have already entered the Great Path; they wish to destroy it, but they shall not succeed in their desire.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In the past, countless eons ago, there was a brahmin whose wife was named Padmā. She was exceptionally beautiful and upright; her countenance was exquisite, her physical form was supreme, and she was a rarity in the world, such that her fame and virtue were beyond compare."

That brahmin had a maidservant whom he associated with and treated with affection and respect; he was unwilling to show reverence to his wife Padumāvatī and took no pleasure in seeing her. Instead, following the words of the maidservant, he led his wife out of the house.
Upon reaching the mountain, he climbed an udumbara tree, selecting the ripe fruits to eat himself while discarding the unripe ones to give to his wife.
His wife asked him,
"For what reason do you alone eat the ripe fruits, casting the unripe ones down and bringing these to me?"
Her husband replied,
"If you wish to obtain ripe ones, why do you not climb the tree yourself and gather them?
His wife answered:
"If you do not give it to me, I shall not obtain it;
I must follow my husband's command.
The wife then immediately climbed the tree.

Seeing his wife climbing a tree, he immediately descended and surrounded the tree on all four sides with thorny brambles, intending to prevent her from getting down; having placed her upon the tree, he abandoned her and departed, wishing for her to die right there.
"At that time, the king, together with his various ministers, went out on a hunting excursion and passed beneath that tree.
Seeing the woman there—so upright and exceptionally beautiful, with such extraordinary features rarely seen in the world—he immediately asked her: 'Who are you? "
"From where have you come?
The wife then explained to the king, from beginning to end, the reason for her transformation.
When the king beheld the woman, he saw that she was endowed with every female characteristic and free from all blemishes; he thought to himself:
"That brahmin is foolish and ignorant; he is no man at all to fail to respect and delight in this woman.
Having cleared away the thorns, she took her away and, upon reaching the inner palace, established her as the queen.

Thereafter, her wisdom and eloquence became difficult to equal; she played with both *chupou* and *liubo*, and her literary compositions were refined and sharp. Women from near and far came to join her in gambling games, yet the Queen always emerged victorious, and none could withstand her.

At that time, the brahmin heard from afar that the king had a queen who was both beautiful and skilled at games of chance; whoever came to play, the queen would emerge victorious, and all submitted to her, none being able to defeat her.
He thought to himself:
"This is none other than my former wife; she was the foremost at dice among my former wives.
Furthermore, that brahmin was also skilled at dice and wished to go before the king to display his skill.
At that time, when the queen heard that the appearance of a certain brahmin was such as this—his facial features, height, and whether he was handsome or ugly—she immediately thought to herself:
"This is my former husband."
At that time, the brahmin went to the gate of the royal palace. The king saw him from afar and tested his skill at dice;
his attendant was named Danta. Then the brahmin spoke in verse:
“His hair is beautiful and eight feet long, And his eyebrows are like a painted stroke.”
"Supremely soft and pliant, one should contemplate it as being like a ripe fruit.
Thereupon, the queen replied with a verse:
"In former times, when I was a maidservant, my will was set upon what I desired."
"Reverence is foremost; taking by force is foremost.
Then the brahmin again answered the queen in verse:
"Go to the place where the dragon dwells in seclusion, where the dragon-elephant constantly roams."
"Amuse yourselves with those signs; you should remember the ripened fruit.
The Queen replied to the brahmin in verse:
"I eat the ripe fruit alone; I cast away the unripe for you."
"This is due to my past causes and conditions; it has been seized by the brahmin.
At that time, the brahmin harbored resentment in his heart, immediately reproaching himself, but his regret came too late to avail anything.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The brahmin at that time was this present lay devotee;
his wife was this present wife."
"The king of that country was none other than myself.
The rebellion that arose at that time is just like this one now.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was no one who did not rejoice.
55. The Sūtra on Parables Spoken by the Buddha. Fifth and Fifty-fifth. In the past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a widow whose livelihood consisted of selling sesame oil and ointments.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, day after day, took sesame oil from his mother to light lamps for the Buddha, continuing this for many years.
Later, the Buddha bestowed a prediction upon the bhikṣu, saying:
"In the future, you shall become a Buddha; the devas, kings, and people shall all go to congratulate you."
The bhikṣu said, "I have received your grace.
Upon hearing that the bhikṣu had conferred the prediction of enlightenment upon her, the widow went to the Buddha's presence and said:
"This bhikṣu who lights the sesame oil lamp is my own; I pray that the Buddha will grant me a prediction [of future enlightenment] as well.
The Buddha said, "When this bhikṣu becomes a Buddha, you shall receive your prediction from him."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The bhikṣu at that time was the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
the mother who lived alone was my own self."

Long ago, in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, there was an elder who, hearing that the Buddha had come to convert beings, went at once to the Buddha’s dwelling. He prostrated himself, touching his head to the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wish to invite the Buddha for a period of three months.”
The Buddha silently consented.
He immediately adjusted his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the house of the elder.

Those who had invited him previously were unable to receive him again; they all gave rise to resentment and plotted to harm the elder. They then set a date, raised their troops, and surrounded the house with several layers of encirclement.
The elder was struck with awe and fear; his mind was fixed single-mindedly on the Buddha, free from any other thought.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, using various essential words of instruction, whereby the elder and his retinue all attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha rose from his seat and went out to address those outside, speaking of the bitter retribution for anger and malice, and praising the blessings of harmony and compassion.
Through these various essential words, the minds of the assembly were enlightened; eighty-four thousand people conceived the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
"In this great assembly, we have seen the Buddha and our minds are liberated; is this because we have encountered the right time, or is it due to causes and conditions from former lives?"
The Buddha said,
"In this assembly, those who are being liberated all at once do so because they have all previously shared karmic conditions with the Buddha.
A bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha will explain this from beginning to end, so that those who hear it may increase their merit.
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a kingdom situated near the great ocean. At that time, the king was named Sāṃdhāna; he governed the country with compassion, regarding his people as his own children."
The kingdom was struck by a great calamity; for three years there was no rain, and the people were suffering from famine.
The King summoned brahmins and practitioners of the Way and asked whether it would rain.
The diviners replied:
"Only after ten years have passed will there be rain!
Upon hearing these words, the king feared that the people would perish; filled with grief and distress, he was ill at ease, thinking:
"What plan should I devise to save my subjects?"
He further thought to himself:
"I must offer my very body as a gift to save all sentient beings!
Thereupon, having purified himself through fasting and observance of the precepts, he joined his palms toward the ten directions and said:

"By virtue of the wholesome deeds I have performed throughout my past and present lives, if there be any karmic reward, I pray that I may be born in the great ocean as a fish of immense body, providing its flesh as an offering to the assembly."
He then closed his mouth and refused to eat.

After seven days, his life ended, and he was reborn as a fish four thousand *li* in length. Possessing the knowledge of past lives, he cast himself upon the seashore, appearing exactly like a black mountain.
When the people saw the mountain, they wondered how such a thing could exist.
They all went to look at it and realized it was a great fish.
The entire nation went there, caught and ate it, thereby escaping their hunger and distress; the country was subsequently restored, becoming as prosperous and fertile as before.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"The fish at that time was my own self;
those who ate my flesh at that time are the people of the city of Vaiśālī today."
In the past, the Tathāgata sustained sentient beings with flesh, but only for the duration of a single lifetime.

Now, by means of the wisdom of the Way, he rescues and protects their consciousness, restoring it to its original state of non-being, so that they may forever depart from the three realms and all suffering shall be eternally extinguished.
The Bodhisattva diligently fulfills the three kinds of giving.
What are the three kinds of giving?
They are external giving, internal giving, and great giving; these are the three kinds of giving.
Clothing, food, precious treasures, kingdoms, wives, and children constitute external giving.
Limbs, body parts, flesh, bones, head, eyes, marrow, and brain constitute internal giving.

The four immeasurables and the six perfections, the impermanence of the four truths, and the twelve divisions of the scriptures—teaching these for the sake of sentient beings constitutes the "Great Gift.
As for the method of seeking the Way, when the three kinds of giving are fully perfected, one will swiftly attain Buddhahood.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, countless sentient beings all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
The elder Śūra, having been thus transformed, converted five thousand people.
Veyśya was young, yet his wisdom was profound and far-reaching; he traveled through various lands, teaching and transforming sixty thousand people, eventually meeting with Śūdraka.
When Śūdraka’s disciples saw that Veyśya possessed such courageous wisdom, they all desired to go and revere him.
Śuddhodana said to the various scholars,
"Vipassī is young, and his wisdom is but slight.
Vipassī overheard these words.
“The Dharma of a Bodhisattva is that one should provide mutual offerings and travel through various lands, regarding them as if seeing the Buddha.
Now, though I am without protection, I shall give rise to the intention of being a fellow-practitioner of the Dharma.”
That very night, Vaira silently departed from that land.
Why was this? It was because he wished to cause those who study to make offerings to Śūḍa.
Because Śūradatta habitually slandered his preceptor, he fell into the Mahānaraka hell for sixty kalpas; having emerged from there and attained human form, he remained tongueless for sixty kalpas.
Why is this? Because they did not restrain their mind, speech, and thought, they lost the Bodhisattva-dharma.
Once their transgressions were exhausted, they attained their former merit and spontaneously achieved Buddhahood, receiving the name Śākyamuni.
The Buddha told the practitioners:
"He who was Shouta is none other than myself; he who was Weixian is now the present Amitābha Buddha.
All those seated there then spoke in unison:
"The fault may be small, yet the transgression incurred is very great.
The Buddha told those gathered:

"One must not fail to guard one's body, speech, and mind. Those who have faith and practice accordingly shall attain the Way. As for the evils and transgressions they have committed, if they can personally recognize them, repent, and confess, their offenses may be slightly lightened."
In the past, during incalculable kalpas, there was a man who extensively practiced giving, making offerings to countless thousands of non-Buddhist brahmins.

Over the course of several years, according to the custom of those brahmins, he who knew the most scriptures was entitled to be the senior seat-holder (*upasthāyaka*). Among them was a brahmin of advanced age and great wisdom, who was the foremost in that assembly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was also in the mountains, studying various scriptures and arts, being erudite in everything.

He would come to attend the assembly and sit at the end of the row; then, one after another, he would inquire about what they knew, and they were unable to surpass him, even reaching the most senior monk.

It was asked: "The knowledge possessed by you, Elder Brahmin, is not even equal to that of the youth; twelve years have already nearly passed [in his studies]. One who knows many scriptures should be given gifts consisting of nine kinds of items."

The nine kinds of objects are: gold, a horse, silver, a saddle, a bridle, a beautiful woman, a golden water-pitcher, a golden basin, and a bed and mat of gold and silver—all of exquisite quality. Such are the nine kinds of objects.
The elder brahmin then thought to himself:
"For twelve years, there has been no one who could rival me; yet this youth has suddenly surpassed me—this is a cause for shame."
"Things are insufficient to express it, and losing one's name is not easily remedied. He then said to the youth:
"The nine items you have offered shall all be given to you; you must lower yourself slightly so that I may be above you."
The youth replied:
"I act according to my own principles and do not force myself to be above others; if I know myself to be inferior, I will naturally remain below, without any cause for regret."
The brahmin was distressed and yielded his seat to him; it was adorned with the seven treasures and was exceedingly exquisite.
The elder brahmin then asked the youth: "In your studies, what do you seek?"
He replied, "I seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in order to deliver and liberate the myriad people.
The elder brahmin, feeling bitter resentment arise in his heart, made a silent vow within himself:
"I shall, in every lifetime, destroy your resolve so that you cannot achieve it; even if you intentionally become a Buddha, I shall surely disrupt it.
He further thought:
"The paths of good and evil diverge; I fear we shall not meet. Only by greatly cultivating virtue can we encounter one another."
He then practiced the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and concurrently cultivated all manner of virtues, never having the slightest intention to abandon them.

Thereupon he departed; the patron gave nine items to the various brahmins, instructing each to divide them among themselves. Once they had done so, each person reduced their share by one silver coin and pursued the youth, saying:
"Do not accept these nine items; let us all share in them together."
Having received [the teachings], the Confucian youth departed each in his own direction.
When the Bodhisattva attained the Way, Devadatta constantly followed him, being born and dying together with him as brothers, yet he constantly sought to ruin the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the elder brahmin was Devadatta;
the youth was Śākyamuni Buddha. Because of their original vow, they have never been separated from one another; such is the beginning and end of their relationship.
The Master said:
"In one's studies, one must have a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Long ago, there was a donkey whose master constantly ordered it to accompany a horse; in eating, drinking, walking, and coming and going, it was always with the horse."
If the horse travels a hundred li, it also travels a hundred li; if the horse travels a thousand li, it also travels a thousand li. Its fur and coat are fine, and its voice is like that of a horse.

Later, he traveled together with a donkey; in eating, drinking, walking, and coming, he was a companion to the donkey. When the donkey traveled a hundred *li*, he also traveled a hundred *li*; when the donkey traveled a thousand *li*, he also traveled a thousand *li*. His fur, head, and body all became exactly like those of a donkey.
"Alas! Alas! To be born as nothing but a donkey until one reaches old age and death, never again becoming a horse—students are just like this.
If they follow a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), they will progress daily; for those who are diligent, the attainment of the Way is swift."
"If one follows evil associates, one will become increasingly indolent; such indolence leads to perpetual sinking.
Formerly, there was a foreign Brahmin who served the gods by constructing a temple and was fond of making divine images, fashioning their heads out of gold.
At that time, there was a thief who climbed onto the celestial image and pulled at its head, but it did not move at all. He then cried out, "Namo Buddha!
and immediately managed to take the head away.

The next day, the Brahmin discovered the celestial head was missing. When the celestial head had vanished, the people gathered together and said, "The heavenly deity has lost its head; this proves there is no such thing as a god."
A deity addressed a certain brahmin:
"The thief could not obtain my head, so he cried out, 'Namo Buddha!
All the devas were thereby moved with alarm; for this reason, I obtained my head."
The brahmins said, "The gods are not equal to the Buddha!
They all departed to serve the Buddha and no longer served the gods.
Even a bandit, by uttering "Namo Buddha," attained rebirth as a celestial being;
how much more so for a worthy person to utter "Namo Buddha"?
The honored deities of the ten directions dare not oppose it; you must simply practice with diligence and never be indolent.
Long ago, there was a śramaṇa who recited the sūtras day and night. A dog lay beneath his bed, listening to the sūtras with single-minded devotion, no longer thinking of food.
After accumulating [merit] in this manner for many years, when her life ended, she obtained a human form and was born as a woman in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
When she grew up and saw a śramaṇa begging for alms, she ran to him and personally offered him food, rejoicing in this way.
Thereafter, she followed after the śramaṇa, became a bhikṣuṇī, and through diligent practice attained the state of an arhat.
Long ago, there was a king who held a great musical performance outside the city, and all the people of the kingdom went together to witness it.

In the city there was a family whose father was ill and unable to walk. The members of the household supported him together, forcing him to go out of the city; they stopped beneath a tree, for he could not proceed further on his own.
He spoke to his family, saying: "Go ahead and return; once you have come back, then take me home."
At that time, Śakra, King of Devas, assumed the guise of a wandering ascetic and passed by his side;
he then called out to the sick man, "Follow me, and I shall cause your illness to be cured."
Upon hearing this, the man was greatly delighted and rose to follow him.

Śakra then led him up to heaven, to the palace of the Heavenly Emperor, where he beheld golden treasures and precious jewels such as were not found in the world. A thought arose in his mind that he wished to beg for some of them.
Someone said to him,
"You may go and ask for a jar.
The sick man then went before Śakra and said:
"I wish to depart; I pray you, grant me this jar.
Śakra then gave it to him and said to him:
"There is something here that fulfills your wishes.

The patient immediately took it back home; the family members gathered together to examine it, and they obtained whatever gold, silver, and precious jewels their hearts desired. They enjoyed themselves to their heart's content, hosting a great assembly of their kinsmen and all those within and without the household for mutual entertainment.
After he had become drunk and satiated, he took up the jar and kicked it, saying, "I have received your kindness; you have made me wealthy.
He continued to kick and leap about until the jar fell to the ground and broke, so that what he sought could no longer be obtained.
The Buddha’s sutras and precepts are like a precious vase: if one hears them for the first time and practices with diligence, whatever one aspires to will surely be attained;
but if later one becomes slightly lax or arrogant, forgetting the sutras and losing the precepts, it is like a broken vase from which nothing more can be obtained!
Among the women of the Dharma family who wear gold, silver, and pearl rings, there are four ways by which they are reborn in the heavens:
first, when those who have mastered the scriptures hear the sutras and rejoice, they take off their rings and offer them as alms; through this one merit, they attain rebirth in the heavens.

Second, if one sees a śramaṇa from afar and rejoices in the construction of a stūpa or monastery, and offers gifts of gold and silver to assist him, these two merits will lead to rebirth in the heavens.

Third, if there are those who are poor and in distress, upon hearing the Buddha say that giving is the foremost practice, they will understand that through the three types of merit gained by giving, one may be reborn in the heavens.

Fourth, when one falls ill and is approaching the end of life, if someone relinquishes their own possessions as an offering to save one's life, and one personally witnesses this act of giving, then at the end of that person's life, they will die with joy and without fear, attaining rebirth in the heavens.
Therefore, the women of the Dharma family have four practices; by wearing gold, silver, and precious rings, they attain rebirth in the heavens.
